tier1.body: Matt--It will be a new, stand-alone, self-contained rulebook.  I am reworking it to get rid of the ambiguities and to make it easier to learn and follow.  The rules are being reformatted but THE RULES CONTENT IS NOT CHANGING.

tier1.author: chezhinkle
tier1.body: @OldProspector Green missiles *only* attack land targets. The range is fixed: one for NATO, two for WP.Quote:17.19 Attacks Against Land TargetsLand targets can be attacked by cruise missiles and bombs. Bothsides have dedicated land attack cruise missiles which have agreen background and can only be used against land targets.I do understand that.  But black and yellow missiles can also attack land targets.  What I am trying to nail down is exact ranges, including ranges versus facilities.  Erik's answer sounds as if a bonus zone (adjacent) is gained when attacking a facility.  I do not think he intended that (and I thank him for helping out), but this illustrates the importance of precise language.From what I understand, all missiles can fire at targets in their same zone, to include land targets connected to their zone (such as Norfolk with West 9-10).  The exception is that US green missiles can be fired from an adjacent zone (West 7-8 vs. Norfolk), and Soviet green missiles can be fired from two zones away (Mid 4 vs. Norfolk).  Is this correct?  (Yes, I know that US missiles would not be fired at Norfolk--I just want to get at the concept of RANGES.)  :-)I am creating a master chart of every type of missile, what nation uses them, what they can be used against, and their ranges.  The variety and use of Missiles is one of the points of confusion that I am addressing.Thanks for any help.

tier1.author: chezhinkle
tier1.body: Very good.  Thank you both for the answers.By this answer "And when striking land targets, the adjacent zone." do you mean that the facility/land target must be connected to the zone?As an example, black missiles fired at Norfolk NS must be fired from West 9-10 and no other zone.  Is that correct?I am actually working on Blue Water Navy Pacific for Compass Games and I am trying to get more precise language into the rules.  This is why I am asking.

tier1.body: Tons of math I had to dig around in my notes but I found the details:1 x Clem/Foch -> Capital (only one because the other is in refit)1 x Aconit (but a single unit) **1 x Cassard (1989) **6 x Commandant Riviere  @3 x George Leygues (Crotale)1 x Suffren **2 x Tourville **11 x D'estienne D'Orves @The double stars are the mixed unit, so it's all the good stuff really:1 x Aconit (but a single unit) **1 x Cassard (1989) **1 x Suffren **2 x Tourville **4 hulls (5 in 1989) at a readiness of 66% (which is the number I used) is only 3 ships, so i actually gave it a bump and added in some George Leygues to make up the numbers with crotale rated (generously) as somewhat effective - which is shall we say.. dubious against something like an AS-4!Unfortunately, the @ ships don't have any SAM capability and only serve to carry Exocet equivalents, so in the scope of the game they are pretty much just targets, as such, i missed them out or assumed they were there but just didn't have very much effect - they were a large part of the overall surface force.You are right about Jean d'arc though, that could have been an extra helo carrier.Overall the French navy IS underrepresented.. but, it just wasn't very effective in the time period of the game (that's not a slight to the no-doubt very brave & effective seamen, rather that their equipment was old and not designed for this scale of conflict).The best French assets are the ones you never see - the nuke boats, and the hunter killers, which are very good - as well as the diesels.

tier1.body: Jimmy Liang  @BravoCo To clarify, the "1 ship only" limitation applies to Soviet white & red missiles or NATO blue missiles.Soviet yellow and black missiles do not suffer from such limitation.Curious what the reasoning is behind that.Why are long range missiles able to fire as a single salvo, but shorter-range missiles unable to?Hi, it's because of the scale of the game - a Nato missile has a 1980's range of 30-60 nmi. If we average that out to something around 50, that is about the width of your little finger on the map, if that. Comparatively, the big Soviet long-range missiles can shoot about 6 times as far - therefore it's much easier to get a load of platforms all into range together. Even allowing NATO missiles at all is generous at this scale to be honest - we are talking about an entire task force engaging an enemy task force at approx 50 nmi. There are so many things that have to go right to even line up that kind of an attack that the odds are not very good.

tier1.threadTitle: Does the rule book make this a non buy?

tier1.author: stuuk
tier1.body: Hi Myles, as the designer of course I can't really be impartial on this. But what I would say is that this is a complex game - a full run of the campaign is something like 8-12 hours of play. But to get there you have to 'get' the systems, and to do that you have to put in the time to learn them.By which I mean, play the intro scenarios and read the examples. If you do that you will find a fun game here. But if you only jump in, you will find frustration. To be ready to play the campaign, you really need to spend 3-6 hours in the scenarios first, and that's not really a bad thing - they're pretty fun in their own right. Your investment in time will be rewarded by a great campaign experience.That's about as neutral as I can be - of course I really like the game, and I know that people don't particularly like the rule book, but the main issue is that the game is quite different in how it works - there are no phases for example. No 'search phase'.  Everything is structured around player actions. But, once you get the game and understand it, you can play it mostly from the quick reference sheets with only occasional rule book flippery.

tier1.author: stuuk
tier1.body: Hello,The answer to most of your queries here is very simple - geography fails on my part, and some 'artist at work' issues likely too. But ultimately i carry the can as the designer.All ports where you get a bonus are shown on the map with a little circle.The thing to remember about the ports is they were really selected as the 'centre of port areas' - in reality there are many ports, and it's likely a convoy would probably split  and spread out over the available ports in the region, so really it's more 'the french ports here' but it was better to name them for the sake of theme and interest.The bonus for port delivery is a mixture of logistical and danger assessments. If you got exactly the same for delivering to Southern France, why deliver to Italy?The answer may come in the form of Soviet mines. But I also figured that being closer was better, and again the Southern placement of the Italian port is only representative - the most crucial supplies would go to the closest port that could take them at that time.The French nukes aren't represented (though if you wish you can assume they're in use) - but in the scenario you propose it would be the French kicking off a nuclear world war three. I dunno about that. In the 60's maybe, but in the 80's I'm not so convinced. He who fires the first of those should expect to receive in kind, and if your two big mates with those weapons are telling you to back down, I don't know. It would have been an interesting option though.Give it a try as you suggest and let us know how it goes?Stu.

tier1.body: Hi Nicolas,The Daphne represents 6 submarines, while the Agosta represents 3. Thus, the Agosta are both more effective and more survivable versus their older sisters - but the Daphne gets a nice 'wolfpack' punch to make them dangerous as well (but they do die pretty quickly).Subs - if you remember playing 688, the missions always started with a radio transmission saying 'hey the Russians are around here somewhere'That's because on its own even a fabulous 688 is only going to hear those Russians maybe 10-15nmi away. The game would be pretty boring if the sub driver never found the targets - and that requires targeting!An airborne radar can see 150-200nmi in every direction, and so is probably 10-20x more effective. And you can move it 300-400 nmi in an hour and look again. An airborne detection platform is enormously more effective in terms of area coverage.A 688 looking 15nmi in every direction lets say would take several hours to cover a 100nmi square box.An equivalent search plane would do it in minutes.Cheers,Stu.

tier1.author: stuuk
tier1.body: My fault, working on finishing one game while giving (poor) rules advice on another!The answer though is option oneMy rambling thoughts below on why that is true...Let's see what the rules say. Relevant bits:6.9: a land area is an area containing ports and/or airfields... with the icons showing adjacency17.3 CAP may roll to attack when... Carrier based fighters defend every Task Force in the Sea Zone and every land facility adjacent to the zone (the carrier does not have to be a target).  Land based fighters protect land bases in their zone (but not Task Forces out at sea). So the problem here really is sloppy wording and definitions.Carriers protect everything adjacent to their sea zone. (easy, and clear)Land based FTR protect everything in their [land] zone. ie: land bases  (this should say land area)The key point here really is that the 6.9 definition of a land zone/area isn't very clear.The intention was that the land-based FTR capability was restrictive. They defend their own base and anything close and that's all, so you've been playing it correctly.If i were to design this again I would have arrows from a base showing which other bases it protects. How much simpler would that have been?!

tier1.body: To be honest more Harpoon than Fleet, which personally I don't feel really gets detection right - in particular with submarines (though that's likely just my personal bias).And the rest of it was actually more math and working out what I thought was a reasonable basis - what is a poor detection? what does it need to be to be a 'good' detection? I spent quite a bit of time working out what an actual bear stalk of a carrier group would look like and then trying to boil that down to just a few rolls of the die.Oddly, the Napoleonic game - 1807(?) where the task forces are blocks and are hidden was probably a bit of an inspiration as well  - I wanted the double-blind guessing game to be in there a bit as well which was done well there by GMT.

tier1.author: stuuk
tier1.body: Hi Daniel, thanks for posting - i always like design questions In general, detection in the game implies an element of 'shadowing' - so a good detection by a Bear-D for example implies that the Bear is doing that pretty continuously until the detection comes off.  It's not quite the same as wwII though where surface ships would shadow one another, at the edge of gun range - that would be unlikely to happen in modern combat - everyone can reach out to the horizon with missiles, and shadowing would reveal you as much as them so would be inherently dangerous - ideally in modern combat, you want to be out of sight and out of mind. Even turning on your radar is best avoided if possible.In terms of submarines, a detection by one might imply some of this as well.I haven't been prescriptive about what exactly it means though - maybe it was just a very accurate contact report, maybe there's a 688 shadowing the group. I decided it was a bit below the level I wanted to go for this game overall.Maybe if i do a more zoomed-in game, I would include something similar. It's certainly an interesting mechanic.

tier1.threadTitle: Campaign Games-Can the Soviet Player win??

tier1.author: stuuk
tier1.body: Hmm it's a difficult one. I did try to make the game 'even' more or less, but within the historical scope - two things that aren't really compatible...I would say strategy can play a big part of course, but at the end of the day your USSR assets are going to get pulverized. It's really only a question of time and whether they can do the job in the interim. Winning early is good. Holding forces back and winning late is also possible, and might be a good thing to try - hunt the NATO SSBNs, go clear out some US attack subs - they can be killed and NATO does not like to lose those, not one bit. Get your RORSATs up, and only attack when you have overwhelming odds or great cards, don't hang about under the ASW airplanes.The hard part for the Soviet is the mid-game, turns 4-8, where if you have been heavily contesting and attacking convoys, you will be feeling the pain and starting to look at an uphill battle.I do personally feel that the game is winnable as the Soviet, but I haven't really collected stats on this in terms of win/lose percentage. I would guess that the Soviet has around 40% chance to win assuming you know the rules and don't make any key strategic blunders.Maybe try an alternate victory condition: if you have 3 hammers and sickles at the end of the game, it's a Soviet minor victory.or if you'd prefer to roll dice, use the above and roll one die per box you are away from coup! on the stability track. If any of the dice are nine or ten, you negotiate a minor victory.

tier1.body: Let's look at the Southern track: if there are two carriers operating in the Med:NATO first need to roll against the track defences on the "Striking Soviet Troops" table. tier1.author: stuuk
tier1.body: Small scenarios have only one day - there is no 'next day' event.The start of the scenario book says this - does it answer your questions?How to use the smaller scenarios 1-5 Ops TrackScenarios 1-5 are all in 1983 by default. Scenarios 1-5 use theOperations Points record track shown below, which is smallerthan the one in the main game.It works in exactly the same way, with events triggering once bothsides’ OPS markers reach or pass the relevant box, resolved afterthe action which moved the OPS marker.The only differences are:1. There is no ‘Next Day’ event - when both players haveexpended all of their available Operations Points, it’s the end ofthe turn.2. Some turns start with both sides’ OPS markers already belowone or more event boxes, in which case apply the event(s) rightaway at the start of the turn before either side spends an OPS.For example: in scenario #1, NATO starts on 5 and the Sovietsstart on 7 OPS. Since both sides markers start below the ‘Fast’ and‘Repair’ event boxes, those events happen before either side doesanything. In this case, there are no Fast Task Forces to move andthere is no facility damage to repair, so the Soviet player can goahead and start the turn having resolved the events.

tier1.body: Hi, is it both NATO task forces combining together and then moving North?If it is, then that simplifies detection (you need detect only one task force) and slows NATO down (they'll need to form up, costing the first fast move and some ops). This does however make the task force tough to fight. They aren't quite missile proof, but you'll only get one strike before the Badgers are toast. They are tough as nails in ASW - you'll need the luck of the dice here too. Try using your ships to go and fight them as well, the Shipwrecks can be quite effective, as can sub-launched missiles. Ultimately you only need a hit or two to start reducing it to a manageable target and the US will then consider whether they can afford to keep exchanging.This scenario is really about teaching how to use the different types of attacks and the differences between multiple task forces vs. a single deathstar - try splitting the Russians into at least two task forces - that doubles the detection work the US has to do.Whilst the single task force concept makes it really tough, repeated attacks should take one down every time.It should be noted though that I didn't quite give you enough to do it with airpower alone, so you will have to use all the toys for this one.

tier1.author: stuuk
tier1.body: Hi Eric, I don't think there's any big disagreement that the rules could be better in places - there are loose terms and even a few unnecessary or confusing rules. It's a point of work for the second game - I played myself yesterday and was frustrated with my own rulebook when I couldn't find something..It was a difficult rule set to write - it's long and complex and models a lot of really complex stuff, so yeah - it's on my list and worry not, I know it's frustrating when a set of rules doesn't say what it means or doesn't mean what it says.That said, all the answers are in the book - as other have said the book does in fact contain all the rules, but finding them can be hard work, certainly harder than it should be - so my main addition for game2 is additional cross referencing and being more verbose in certain important sections of the rules, like this one.Anyway on to your questions:zones - so yes, 'zones' really means sea zones 'sea areas' the movement spaces etc."Land Area – An area of land adjacent to a Sea Zone.""6.9 Land Areas    These are areas of the map that contain ports and/or airfields," ... "The airfield and port symbols are used to show which Sea Zonesthe facility is adjacent to. Any symbol or airfield/port box touching a Sea Zone indicates adjacency. Exception: The Kola Ports are only adjacent to North 9-10."and"Example: The UK has two facilities. The airfield is adjacent to North 5-6 because Lossiemouth touches the Sea Zone, North 3-4 because Leuchars touches the Sea Zone, East 6 because of Stornoway, and East 4 because the facility box itself touches that Sea Zone"Similarly, a Soviet bomber (or TF) can launch a strike on UK airfield from North 5-6?Yes - they're adjacent, so can be attackedIf the answer to the question is "yes," bombers can launch from North 5-6, then there are two different definitions of adjacency, one for movement from an airbase / port and a different one for strikes against ports and airfields.yes this is correct - "6.12 Measuring RangeFor movement purposes a Land Area is one zone away from alladjacent Sea Zones, however when a facility is being attackedthe attacking units only need to be able to reach an adjacent SeaZone."Maybe the confusion is that ths above parapraph should also be referenced in 6.9, where the concept of adjacency is introduced and discussed?

tier1.author: stuuk
tier1.body: The only navy with the capability to stop a Russian strike is the US, so if you're talking about the UK or France it's simply that they aren't up to the job.US F-14's get 4 dice at +2 DRM.They need a total of 8 or higher to kill Backfire (35% of 2 or more hits; 76% of at least one hit) - and some misses will shoot down missiles.One third of those hits will be an intercept before launch of missiles, which is extra bad for the Russians.The Soviets can claim a 6+ save however if they have a good detection.I wouldn't say that's a very low hit probability - you've only a 1 in 4 of getting in without getting shot. Actually I would say that's a high probability of getting shot.And yes the navy would absolutely chuck them up, but there are lots of limits around this kind of thing - fighters are constantly busy with refuelling, rearming, maintenance, crew changeups. Plus there are only so many catapults and on top of that starting one of these things up takes a bit of time. On a detection the enemy is already likely within 300 miles so it's pretty much too late for the fighters on the deck to do much - they already missed the fight. You have to know the enemy is coming before they get there.

tier1.author: stuuk
tier1.body: Smaller strikes generally get picked up by less defenders - so a multi-regiment strike of 100 backfires is a very big target, probably attacking from multiple points of the compass, whereas a single regiment is a smaller thing to see, and probably attacks from only one vector.You could certainly argue that more defenders = more chance to pickup.But then the inverse would also be true for less attackers.So then you would also have to define how much CAP is needed to adequately defend one area of space around the clock.If there are 24 fighters in a counter, there's not many up at any one time (about 6-8)and how much STK represents an 'average' density of striking aircraft.Initially I had something like:Roll base dice with one unit+1 die per extra fighter on CAP/INT-1 die per enemy unit under 3 (3= 0; 2= -1; 1= -2)or something similar - there was a modifier for density of planes in the air and also something else for FTR detection capability.It was simpler though to go with the rule we ended up with, and the results were not much different so we went with simplicity.All in all your FTR still gets to roll its dice and you can never be confident of not getting hurt, and it's still better to have two FTR in a place versus one - not always but most of the time.

tier1.body: Absolutely - recon sats like the Soviet RORSAT are close to the Earth, and so not geostationary - they cannot be placed above a choke-point. So what you end up with is a ground track that repeats every 12 hours or similar - you have large bands of the earths surface that a satellite will cover on its first pass then another band on the second pass and so on.This means to fully cover a particular place you need multiple satellites all going over that place at different times.Then even with that there's to problem of getting the data back to where it's needed - if doing that takes as little as an hour, your target could be off by 30 miles, clearly longer is worse.And then you have the weather..All of this adds up to make it a very useful tool, but one that cannot be guaranteed to produce the result.

tier1.author: stuuk
tier1.body: Hi Thomas, Back in the 80's it's likely some platforms could do this but they would be specially adapted, and then the special platforms would have to pass that info out by other means like regular radio.Today - yes I'm sure that a variety of platforms can do this and then data-link it out to some others.Even then though, there's not a ship today built without RADAR and carriers all have recon planes, so that tells you something about the need for them. I don't think navies will ever not want their own detection assets, after all satellites can be shot down or jammed, or hacked, or blinded.Satellite detection is very powerful but it's not (like anything else) the only answer to the problem and any one problem can be countered - resilience is good.

tier1.author: stuuk
tier1.body: Hi James, lets have a look at the real life figures first:10 SA-2 batteries sounds formidable, but the Fan-Song engagement radar can control only one missile in the air at one time.Even accounting for the possible addition of secondary radars and so on, the number is 10-20, plus maybe a few more outbound.There was an SA-5 up there (maybe two I forget now) with the nuclear rounds as well and the super-long range missiles.And 1-2 SA-10 launchers in any period of the game - they account for the majority of the 'useful' fire.They have FLAP LID engagement RADAR - 6 simultaneous targets.So.. if we say that against the raid everyone gets two shots just for easy math we have:10 SA-2 (ROF 1) * 2 shots = 202 SA-10 (ROF 6) * 2 shots = 24=44Divide this by 16 to get SAM points = 2.7, so I gave the Russians a bit extra and rounded up. Though..- The above assumes even shots per battery which is unlikely but more to the point..- It doesn't account for the almost certain on-the-deck profile of the strike, which would reduce detection range to 10-15nmi meaning less shot opportunities.- The SA-2 was probably really crappy+ The SA-10 missiles might have been able to home once in the air without their director+ This doesn't account for any of the shenanigans of the defending PVO fighters, but it's probably likely they would stay a little way from SAM alleyCountering this we have HARMs and SHRIKEs - anti radiation (RADAR killing) missiles.To shutdown all of the above SAMs would require 1 missile per RADAR - only about 15 missiles, and those SA-10's are getting priority attention.Hit or miss doesn't matter too much - those RADARs are likely being turned off otherwise you lose your ability to shoot at anything because your RADAR is killed.For the duration of the strike you may need double the number of these weapons but the point is that the advantage here is certainly with the US - who practiced and enhanced this technique over Vietnam for many years (and then demonstrated with brutal efficiency over Iraq just after the end of the cold war).In game terms, a single CAG has two bombing dice.If it uses one of those to engage the SAMs then only a single one remains for the actual targets.Two CAGs however have 4 bombing dice and one free dice for the Prowlers.You can't count on the A-6's doing the job alone so you really need to allocate 1-2 of those bombing dice to kill SAMs, or risk it.That only leaves two or three dice for the actual targets.I suspect you are playing that those SEAD dice are 'free' attacks? which is not the case - any ammo used on SEAD is not used on targets.Oh and yes, the SU-15, TU-128 etc are all built into the MIG-23 counters - they just got a bit of an upgrade ;0Stu

tier1.author: stuuk
tier1.body: Yes exactly that, originally we had two rolls way back when - detection and then attack.Ultimately for ease of play it was all rolled into one roll - many Soviet subs are killed on an 8, while the US SSNs need 10's.And many of those get a 6+ 'save' against any hit taken as well.I do sometimes see people asking about the old 'fleet' submarine detection - but realistically, in a war scenario the only reason to detect an enemy sub is to try and sink it or avoid it - the idea of keeping a sub detected for extended periods and trailing them absolutely applies in peacetime, but in wartime you're going to setup your shot and get those fish in the water, not mess about tracking it - that's just asking for trouble.

tier1.author: stuuk
tier1.body: Boom or Bust – an AAR all about the Blue Water Navy 1st Scenario – or how I learned to hate the Tigerfish.By Vadeem Redpath.Faced with spending more time in the basement than I had envisaged over the last little while, I decided to pull out  Blue Water Navy from Compass Games and give it a go. I had been a playtester for this game in 2018/19 and then had a couple of goes on Vassal, but due to circumstances beyond my control, never really got to play the full campaign.The idea was to play the 1st scenario solo and remind myself of the mechanisms, as a prelude to a full naval slugfest later. The first scenario is called “The Boomer Bastion”The scenario is simple really, the 3rd WW has started just a few days ago and the NATO strategy is to de-fang the Russian nuclear threat by sending in nuclear attack submarines into the Boomer Bastion in the North Barents sea, and sink the Russian nuclear missile submarines (The Boomers)  hiding there. There is a secondary defensive objective for NATO, which is to prevent the Soviets sending a pack of attack submarines through the GIUK gap, the sea bits between Greenland, Iceland and the UK.The Russian objective is to defend the ‘Boomers’ and to break out the attack subs to sink NATO convoys in the North Atlantic. To assist in either attack or defence the Russians also have a small Kiev Carrier Group, that starts in port,  with a few good ASW ships, and some close range fighters that can shoot down stuff that gets too close but are pretty weak otherwise.Both sides have MP (Maritime Patrol ) aircraft squadrons to assist, NATO in the UK, and the Russians on the kola peninsular, but these aircraft are no use in the Arctic Sea area as the subs hide under the ice pack. Last but not least both of the areas of interest, the GIUK Gap, and the boomer Bastion have a lot of sensor arrays and local patrols that can cause a submarine that crosses/enters the area, to be subject to attack form patrolling subs, or light patrols not represented by any counters.The scenario is only 3 turns long, but each turn has 7 Operations Points for the Soviets, and 5 for the NATO player. More on this later, but that seemed at the start of the game to be a lot of Ops Points, as they are used to move and do combat with air and sub assets only, but as we shall see, you can never have enough Ops Points.The start of the scenario is pre- set except for the weather and the event Cards. At the start of the game the weather is rolled for, and at the start of each turn, and players draw 5 cards that can only be used for the reaction events – this is different to the main game but adds a bit of variety. See above a snapshot of the game set up. In the lower right of the shot are the USSR air and naval bases on the Kola peninsular, the UK have a bunch of MP assets over the GIUK gap, and the Norwegian diesel subs, supported by a USN hunter killer sub group hunting some USSR Alpha submarines in the Norwegian Sea. Just NE of Iceland lurk a UK sub Group and a November class sniffing around each other. A USN Sturgeon Group is under the Arctic Ice and the rest of the soviet  boomers and defending USSR subs are in the Bastion Turn 1: The weather rolls resulted in bad weather in the Barents Sea, and the Norwegian Sea, but clear elsewhere. Bad weather represents storms and the like and mean that surface ships go slower, and that MP have a reduced attack capability vs submarines due to the crap conditions. This meant that both NATO and Russia would have a hard time prosecuting subs in those zones with ASW aircraft, and that the Soviet Carrier Group would have to fight through a northerly gale to get out of the ports in Russia.Soviet player card draw was not too bad, 3 cards of no use, and 2 that might be useful during the game, remember just the Reaction Event is in playing these short scenarios, so the Tigerfish, and Counter Attack might be useful. NATO player card draw was useless , with not one card that could be used to affect any Soviet activity in this short scenario, so I will not even show them!When playing solo I like to use a method that Donald Featherstone invented ages ago, I have a look at the situation for the side at hand, their objectives, the forces that they have and do a quick combat appreciation – then  make a small table of choices of possible plan – up to 6 , and then roll a dice to decide on the basic strategy they are trying to carry out. I try to balance aggressive, moderate and defensive choices so either side can be a bit gung ho, or more conservative, depending on the dice roll..In this case for  the Soviets I decided that they would either play very defensive, with the Task Force and the ASW aircraft trying to defend the Boomers, and forego the possibility of a break out – or  they would do the opposite, go all out offensive -  let the boomers take their chances, even splitting up and running out of the Bastion, and send everything at the GIUK gap.  The die roll said to play defensive, so that is how I played the Soviets during the game. For NATO it is less clear cut, they had superior submarines, but the Bastion is not able to be attacked by the MP, so I rolled for a strategy and it came out balanced: leave the Norwegian diesel subs and the MP’s to stop any Russian breakout, and have everyone else go for the Bastion, trusting to God and Lockheed Martin to carry the day.Each turn alternates using operations points, or passing - with the Soviet going first.Turn 1 – without going into excruciating detail on every dice roll, the Soviets formed up the Carrier Task force, sortied it into the Barents Sea in the really bad weather,  and sent out the Maritime ASW aircraft into the Norwegian Sea to try and get the Norwegian diesel boats. The Red attack submarines attacked any nearby NATO subs and then fell back under the Arctic and into the Boomer Bastion, sheltering behind all of the sonar arrays and the patrolling ASW corvettes.NATO moved all of their attack subs forward, attacking where they had a chance, and ended up with two attack  Groups under the Arctic ready to attack into the Bastion on Turn 2.This was partially successful, for both the Soviets and NATO. The noisy November class hunter killer in the North Norwegian Sea was dinged by the UK Swiftsure before she got away, and the Norwegian diesel boats were sunk after being attacked by the Alpha, followed by successive waves of Russian ASW Bears, despite the bad weather. (They had nothing better to do). The ay was sent North to reinforce the Bastion ASW patrols (put on patrol)The situation at the end of Turn was looked like this: Turn 2: The Penetration of  the BastionTurn 2 was a case of brute force as the NATO submarines attacked into the Bastion, and the Russians defended. The weather was pretty much the same as the 1st turn, but the weather in the Barents Sea improved, the Norwegian Sea was poor.As the stealthy NATO subs transited into the Bastion they were attacked by the lurking defending Soviet attack subs, all getting one extra die as they were alerted by the sonar arrays and local patrols. The NATO subs all moved in and attacked boomers if they got the chance. The Russian TF moved into the Boomer Bastion, and added it’s local ASW attack capability to the lurking ASW subs. A few things to watch for if you are new to BWN, there are a few special rules for the Boomer Bastion, namely that  attacking subs alerted by the sonar arrays get an extra die to roll. This might not seem a big deal, but as they are equipped with Rocket ASW capability, any time they attack and get a double below 10 in value then it causes a step loss, no matter what the defence strength of the NATO sub they are attacking..  increasing from 2 to 3 die, can make that a slightly more likely occurrence, representing the use of missile carried torpedoes, cued by the passive sonar arrays. NATO subs had no tactical counter to that at the time of the game setting, except for being vewy, vewy quiet, and therefore would have to run and throw out decoys, in BWN represented by the saving roll if they are ‘hit.’The Soviet Maritime ASW was useless, 9 dice rolled vs the subs in the Bastion, and not a single hit! Followed up by a useless hunt by the Soviet TF, also not getting a single hit.Every NATO sub that was entering the Bastion had to run the gauntlet of Soviet subs cueing in on them and attacking. Only the very high defence strength of the NATO subs (10 in every case) saved them, but one of the Los Angeles boats was sunk, (flipped a counter in the game terms). After the Bastion attacks the NATO subs managed to sneak through and sink a full counter of Deltas, and damage another one. A victory for the NATO player is to get 8 nuclear payload points sunk, with the slower and noisier Deltas being worth 4, the Typhoon a whopping 8, and the in between Delta 3’s at 6 each. So at the end of Turn 2 the NATO side had 6 of the 8 needed. Surely victory was in reachThe end of turn 2 looked like this:   Here lay the problem with Soviet defensive strategy, they have a ton of assets, all of the air, all of the surface vessels, the extra patrols and the extra die for their sub hunter killers in the Bastion, but the defence value of every NATO sub is 10, and the newer subs also get a saving roll if they are hit. So a lot of ‘shots’ are going to be needed to kill the NATO subs, before they get a shot at the boomers, and conversely the  NATO attack is +1 for all of their subs , so they have a really good chance of sinking the old Delta I and II boomers that only have a defence of 8.Turn 3: All or NothingThe weather roll was benign, with a storm still blowing in the Norwegian Sea, but nothing in the Barents.  Soviets go first and choose to activate the  Victor III, they will also get to activate the Carrier TF as well, as the Ops counter drops off a ships square, already assumed passed by the NATO Ops counter.With 3 die to roll the Victor gets an 8,8,9. This would normally not get a hit, but remember those funny rocket torpedoes, any double hits a NATO sub regardless of defence value. The Victor 3 also gets a +1 for the tactical acumen displayed by its hand picked crew, and so the final totals are 9,9,10. With another hit for the rocket torps, this is 2 hits, and the Soviet  gets to  allocate the second one, the Defender (NATO) allocates the 1st. NATO allocates the hit to the damaged Los Angeles, destroying her, and the Russian allocates  the next hit to the  other Los Angeles as they are the most dangerous NATO subs.The Soviets now attack with the ASW value of the TF. The ships total up 8 ASW factors, and there is an additional +2 for having  a carrier along (lots of ASW helicopters on the Kiev class) , so   the total number of dice being rolled are 3 with a +1 on every die.They roll 6, 9 and 10. So with the +1 we have a 7, 10 and 10, with the natural 10 being good for the Soviet as they can allocate it first. The N10 is allocated to the Swiftsure, flipping her, and the second is allocated by NATO to the Sturgeon,.  This is a cracking result for the Soviets on Phase 1 as the NATO attack force now only has a 2 die attack each Phase with any submarine.NATO goes next and expends an Ops Point to attack with the Swiftsure , rolling 2 dice to try and kill another Boomer step for the win. A 1 and a 9 looks promising at first sight , until the Soviet side pulls out the dreaded Tigerfish reaction  event card – this stops the 9 from being a hit, and the 1 also kills the Swiftsure, as in the Bastion a Natural 1 is a local kill by the Bastion forces – a paltry Grisha ASW corvette  got lucky.!!!! Soviet Ops Phase  next – and an ops point is expended to bring a Bear to bear, flying in one of the ASW hunting aircraft to try and kill one of the damaged subs. There was a slim choice to try and run the damaged Delta out of the Bastion but the USSR decided to give the maritime air at least one more chance to redeem themselves.  The Bears had had really bad luck so far in this game after sinking the Norwegian diesel subs, and in true style they kept that streak going,  3 dice, and rolls 3, 5 , 5 – nothing!With the damaged US Los Angeles class SSN left for NATO or the Sturgeon, they expend an Ops point and attacked with the Los Angeles.  A roll of 1 and a 5 was catastrophic – not only did they miss the clunky Delta, even with the +1 for good weapons and sonar, but the natural 1 meant that the Grisha , or something like that, killed the step of USN subs.Ops points remaining are 3 for the NATO and 5 for the USSR.The USSR activate the Alpha, having given up all hope of killing anything with the air squadrons, and roll 2 dice, getting a 12 and a 10. The 10 will kill unless the Sturgeon rolls a 6+ to evade,  which it does.Ops remaining 3 for NATO, 4 for USSR. NATO activates the Sturgeon on a last attack  run, attacking and then running for the Arctic….if this doesn’t kill a Boomer for the game win   and then hide under the ice it would have to withstand 2 more ASW air attacks, the ASW Carrier group attack and  a Victor chasing it down. Under the ice at least the air is no use, and the carrier Group can’t chase it down.Rolling 2 dice, +1 to each for the NATO sonar superiority , a 6 ,and a 7 are just enough. The damaged Delta counter goes to the bottom (Defence of 8) …..but in a final twist the USSR plays the counter attack card at the end – which states that if a sub is sunk then the USSR can cause a step loss on a 6+ , which they do and sink the Sturgeon before it can escape.!!  [I am not sure if it should have had a saving roll against this as well, but chose not to for fun as the game was over anyway]So the NATO player wins, but a pyrrhic victory at best, all of the NATO attack subs were sunk, but the USSR boomer fleet is depleted by about 8 missile firing subs.. Conclusion: The game plays fast and easy once you have the basic rules and procedures down, and I only found myself looking up a few odd ball chrome items…more for clarification than anything else, and the majority of the time all you need to play are the Quicksheets. I would perhaps modify the Victory conditions of this scenario – to -1 from the number of Boomer steps for each step loss of NATO nuclear boats lost? This might make for a more competitive game, but I am always wary of changing anything on the basis of one games results -  what if the Bears had been more effective or the attacks as the NATO subs went through the Bastion cordon were more effective…? A game worth trying, and as you can see from the screen shots the Vassal module is also excellent. Enjoy.D

tier1.body: The rationale is that a smaller strike is more difficult to detect in the first place.Initially, I had a detection number for a FTR to respond at all, modified by what was actually happening. A very large strike was almost automatically detected whereas a very small strike flying anti-RADAR (Buccaneers at 30 feet over a forest, in the dark) was very hard to detect and respond to.This was a simplification of that idea which requires less thought and one less table.And, since you're going to choose your best unit to attack with, you effectively already get a DRM bonus - sneaking up on a load of MIG-31 is not so easy with 4 dice at +2; wheras a poor old MIG-21 is more likely to be killed on the ground.

tier1.body: The advantage is that NATO gets to kill missiles, with no chance for the enemy to 'save' kills.It is probably not always a good bet. Take for example at attack where you know you can deal with 6 missiles because of your SAMS but there are twelve incoming - you could use this option, disregarding the bombers and you now have a reasonable chance (3 chances per die, 4 dice) of stopping the attack entirely.If instead you go for the bombers, and roll two N10 results - if the enemy has a good detection they then get a 6+ save. This option therefore gives you an extra 0.5 pips per die chance to kill the missiles.Plus of course a single '3' is a lot of incoming missiles shot down.On the other hand if you don't like the option or feel it doesn't do enough then feel free to ignore it - it's just an optional rule.

tier1.body: Just for fun, we can try seeing what happens if the incoming is a Soviet AS-4. It's a whole different piece of kit as it's moving at 2300 knots - 0.64 nmi per second.This gives a little under 8 seconds before it arrives and now the Krivaks get a single shot. But here's the kicker:	detection at	5	nm	SAM			0.45	nm/secVAMP			0.64	nm/sec			1.09	total closure nm/sec	Total time to hit	7.8125		processing time		3	sec/shot					1st impact takes	4.59				incoming travels	4.86	nm	now at		        0.14	nmBy the time the slower SAM arrives, the missile is only 0.14nm away (250 meters) from the target - so even if the SAM takes it out, your superstructure is very likely going to be peppered with fragments of missile slowing down from mach 4! That would be effectively a kill.This is being generous to the target by the way as the AS-4 would be in a terminal dive anyway and might not even be engageable by this weapon - it's designed to shoot NATO missiles

tier1.author: stuuk
tier1.body: Morning gents, looking at Krivak ASW Group the components are:Krivak I (6)Krivak II (2)  Mod Kildin(2)SSM:The 8 Krivaks are armed with SS-N-14 Silex x 4 each (ASW, secondary anti-surface capability using 185kg warhead)I have assumed that each Krivak has two SSM's loaded for 16 warheads on top of the Mod Kildin.SAM:Krivak: 2x SA-N-4 using Pop Group @ 1600 knots, ~5nmi.Mod Kildin: unarmedAgainst a typical NATO missile moving at 600 knots, we can assume the first shot happens at 5nmi. The Missile has a closure of 0.16 nmi/sec, therefore you have 31 seconds total to impact.The SAM has a closure of 0.45 nmi/sec so you will get several shots at the missile stream over the time it takes to arrive at the target.The total closure of missile and SAM is 0.6 nmi per second.The numbers work out at 3 shots:Note that each calculation also bakes in 3 seconds of 'acquisition time' for mount re-orienting and sensor tracking1st impact takes 8.20 sec (5nmi / 0.6 closure = 8.2)incoming travels 1.79 nmi (0.16)*(8.2+3.0)now at		 3.21 nmi2nd impact takes 5.26 secincoming travels 1.32 nminow at		 1.89 nmi3rd impact takes 3.09 secincoming travels 0.97 nminow at		 0.91 nmiAt that point close-defences have a little under 6 seconds to react.Looking then at three shots per ship. 3Two mounts per ship. 3*2=6Eight ships. 6*8=4848/16=3 SAM pointsThis is assuming 100% of the ships are firing and that they are all together in one location - 66% might be more reasonable and would give a value of 2 versus the theoretical maximum of 3. It also makes no attempt to account for closing/traversing shots or anything else more complex.But, you can see that it's a pretty close approximation for such a high-level strategic game.(and yes I have a calculator for this that I made for the purpose : )

tier1.author: stuuk
tier1.body: Don't mind a bit of conversation on such topics at all.. Also, I may be mistaken but I thought we only had two carriers make it to the Falklands - Invincible and Hermes?And some of that was more luck than judgement in terms of timing (sales to Aus, and one of the CVLs was in post-construction).The problem with maintenance cycles on complex warships is that they tend to be very long - a year is common, and sometimes longer - see the US carrier MLU's for example where the carrier is literally in many many pieces in a drydock.These things cannot generally be thrown back together - and also be either safe or combat worthy - note for example that the UK 'strategic deterrent' is only 1 SSBN at sea with another available to sail, of the three boats we have.Actually, my thinking was that the Soviets probably should have had a higher readiness than NATO - their ships spent most of their lives tied up pierside, not doing round the world tours and port visits. Of course that raises its own problems in terms of crew competency and maintenance having been actually done as it should have been.But I didn't want to get into crew quality - the game is too big for such factors and I have balanced some of that out in the cards (note that the Soviets are more likely to sink their own submarines than NATO..)So ultimately I went with 66-70% (actually some of the Soviet units are working on closer to 75%, so I did give them a small bonus..)because the line has to be drawn somewhere - the air units are about 95% though as airframes are quicker to get ready for combat.

tier1.author: stuuk
tier1.body: Hi all, I am considering a sequel covering the Pacific. Since it came up in another thread, thought I would move it here for discussion on the topic. Dan Beckler  @wedgeantilles1971 I'd vote for a Pacific theater as well, as I cut my teeth on Victory Games 7th Fleet back in '88 - wasn't able to find 2nd Fleet at the time.However I'd wonder what "victory" would look like for the Soviets in that theater in that time.  The 7th Fleet game gave a lot of VPs (if I remember correctly) for getting convoys to Vladivostok and Cam Ranh Bay. But a maximum effort to get to Cam Rahn Bay would involve using both their CVHs and the Kirov-class, stripping their punch from every other mission in the theater to run that gauntlet to Vietnam.  And they would still be up against multiple CVN battle groups.  It seemed as though their real order of battle was geared to defend the Sea of Okhotsk bastion for their SSBNs.I agree that the Pacific fleet was designed for defence, and not sure why taking a convoy to Vietnam would be a thing the Soviets would have particularly wanted to do?Perhaps if the Vietnamese were fighting on land, or else to support Soviet planes already there - but I wouldn't have thought it the cornerstone of a Soviet Pacific strategy.On my list of Soviet potential goals I have:Invade China or pressure China to aid N Korea or invade TaiwanNorth Korean invasion of South KoreaInvade JapanDisrupt the Shipping lanes to Japan / SE AsiaIt could also include 'survive'

It's an option maybe.Future or present day there is no fight, the Russians get sunk so that's not really on the cards.But if you have ideas or requests I would be very happy to hear them!I'm much more interested in the Pacific theater.. but that's getting ahead of myself...Dan great to hear you using the game to teach some history! Gave me a proud feeling that post, thanks!

tier1.body: Hi Louis, I can post some here but it can take a good long while for BGG to approve uploads. There is currently no card art - that's awaiting artist.Here's a flavour of a few of them without the wait time:Spetznaz Assault : Cost 2. Choose any target facility and roll one die on the air to ground bombing table. Remove.Port Mining : Cost 1. Select any available submarine in a zone with an enemy port. Roll one detection die against the submarine per step & prosecute attacks normally (as helo). Mark 'spent'. Place one mine step for each step undetected.Space Shuttle : Cost 1. Roll a die. On a 5+ Remove any RORSAT step of your choice.Snoopers Detect Raid : REACTION Play to place a 'detected' marker on an air strike. Play if there are at least 2 steps of NATO submarines in the sea zone adjacent to the base of origin & Soviet ASAT system is not active

tier1.author: stuuk
tier1.body: Well the rules are posted here on BGG for you to have a look at. They are a little old but they should set the scene.In general the game is a much bigger version of the idea behind 2nd - which covered the GIUK gap and further North. BWN covers right over to the states and also the Med. It also uses a realistic ORBAT and much more of the strategic scope than 2nd.The game is very different from VGs games - this is card driven (except the smaller scenarios), area-based, uses a many-dice approach to combat and minimises charts.It does however produce 'realistic' results in terms of combat and interactions.Do you have any specific questions?

tier2.author: Osirith
tier2.body: Hi all, since a week, I am trying to use IA LLM (Anthropic's Claude) to play solo against IA (that plays Warsaw Pact).I have uploaded rules, tables for zones adjacencies, tables for unit stats, etc to Claude.Result is a mixed bag :BAD :- IA has difficulties thinking long term, and is not very good at finding the best path for units (to avoid Patrols, for examples). Sometimes it works, sometimes not.GOOD :- Overall, IA is using the rules quite well. It even has explained to me a few errors I made (giving the rule exceprt to explain).- I asked Claude IA to use story depictions a bit like Tom Clancy's books (Red October, Red Storm Rising, ...).Overall :Not good enough to play without some help, but very nice to avoid all deciding by myself for both sides, and also to implement the somewhat complex combat rules.You will see a small bit of the scenario 2a as played below.The text in yellow is the text I type myself for my orders. Everything else is generated by IA.The text in cyan is "story driven" by IA.Tell me what you think !!ChrisQuote:### Soviet Action #1 (1 OPS, USSR 9→8)**Event Check:** USSR = 8, NATO = 6 → Case 8 (REPAIR): Both ≤ 8 → REPAIR triggers. No damaged facilities → no effect.**Alfa: Move & Attack (torpedo) → TF RANGER (East 2)**East 3 → East 2 (1 zone). No SOSUS. Alfa arrives Spent. TF RANGER in Good Detection → +1 die.Anti-Surface 2 + 1 (Good Det) = **3 dice**, Tactical +0.*The Project 705 Lira surges from the depths of East 3 like a titanium shark, its UGST torpedoes racing at 50 knots toward the American convoy...***Alfa torpedo dice: [1, 1, 8]**- Die 1: Miss- Die 1: Miss- Die 8: HIT PM/Amph/Convoy- Double 1: No effect in 7.3 torpedo attack (SSM requires Torpedo Technology for Soviet subs, which isn't in play).**1 hit on Convoy.** But first, TF ASW retaliation:**TF RANGER ASW:** US-5 (4) + Convoy (1) + Sturgeon BKD (2x3=6) = 11 → 3 dice, Tactical +1.Alfa is Non-Magnetic: only a natural 10 can hit. Alfa has 6+ save on top. Modified 8+ = disrupt.**NATO ASW dice: [10, 8, 2]** (Tactical +1)- **Die 10: NATURAL 10!** Step loss on Alfa!- Die 8 (+1 = 9): DISRUPT- Die 2 (+1 = 3): Miss**Alfa save roll: 4** — FAILED! **Alfa flipped** (1 step remaining).**Disrupt:** Die 8 (modified 9) gives 1 disrupt. NATO cancels the only remaining attack die (the 8).**Result: Convoy takes NO additional damage. Alfa flipped.***The Mk48 ADCAP from the Sturgeon BKD strikes the titanium hull of the Lira. Even the miracle alloy of Project 705 cannot absorb a heavy American torpedo without damage...*---### NATO Action #1 (1 OPS, NATO 6→5)**P-3 Orion flies from Lajes for ASW attack in East 3**Target: Echo II — Defense 8, no save, not Non-Magnetic. Hit on 8+.**NATO ASW dice: [7, 2, 1]** — All miss (needed 8+).*The sonobuoys detect the Project 675's signature, but the torpedoes pass too far above. The Echo II slips calmly into the thermal layer...*P-3 Orion returns to Lajes, Spent.---### Soviet Action #2 (1 OPS, USSR 8→7)**Event Check:** USSR = 7, NATO = 5 → Case 7 (SHIPS): Both ≤ 7 → **SHIPS EVENT triggers!****Echo II: Move & Attack (missiles) → East 2, TF RANGER**East 3 → East 2 (1 zone). No SOSUS. Echo II launches a **missile attack** (7.4.1.1) — 3 SS-N-12 Sandbox missiles.Good Detection → +1 die. 2 dice (1 base + 1 Good Det), use best.**Echo II missile launch dice: [5, 5]**, best = 5 → **4-7: LONG RANGE attack.** 3 black missiles incoming!Echo II marked Spent and Cruise Missiles Fired.**SAM Defense:** US-5 (4) + Convoy (1) = 5 SAM. 3 missiles → 4 SAMs usable.**NATO SAM dice: [8, 3, 2, 1]**- Die 8: 1 missile shot down- Die 3: 1 missile shot down- Die 2: Miss- Die 1: Miss**2 shot down. 1 remains.****Missile Resolution:** 1 missile, DRM +1 (Good Det). 1-2: Miss, 3-10: Hit.**Soviet resolution die: 5** (+1 = 6) → **HIT!****Allocation dice: [4, 9]** — 9 rolled! Soviet allocates → **CONVOY!**Missiles inflict 2 hits on Convoys. Convoy: 2 + 2 = **4 hits** (Convoy survives — sunk at 5th hit).*The SS-N-12 Sandbox strikes the heart of the transport formation at Mach 2.5...*---### SHIPS Event #3 — Turn 2**TF Movement:**USSR: No TFs.NATO:- TF SHIELD: moves from North 5-6 to Trondheim port and dissolves.- TF RANGER: moves from East to East 4 - TF BRAVO: moves from Mid 2 to Mid 3**AMPHIBIOUS DELIVERED! TF SHIELD retired from the game.** The Royal Marines land in Trondheim. Norway will hold.**Detection Degradation:** TF RANGER: Good → Poor.---### NATO Action #2 — Free Action + OPS**F-4 Phantom Rng 1 recalled from North 5-6** (free), refueled, **redeployed → Patrol in East 4** (1 OPS, NATO 5→4). Directly protecting the wounded TF RANGER.---### Soviet Action #3 (1 OPS, USSR 7→6)**Bear D #1 flies from Kola for detection mission → East 4**Route: Kola → North 9-10 → North 5-6 → North 3-4 → East 4 (4 zones, range 6). Only one Phantom to pass through — in East 4 (CAP).**Interception in East 4:** F-4 Phantom Rng 1 vs MP: 1 die, Tactical +1.**NATO interception die: 5** (+1 = 6) — Miss. Bear D evades.**Bear D detection dice: [1, 9]**- Die 9: **GOOD Detection placed by Soviet player!**TF RANGER upgraded to **GOOD Detection.** Full composition revealed.Bear D returns to Kola, Spent.**Bonus Action (5.3.1):** The active player may immediately attack the detected TF!**Backfire + 2 Badger + Tanker → Massive strike on TF RANGER (East 4)**Route: Kola → North 9-10 → North 5-6 → North 3-4 → East 4 (4 zones).Tanker (2 steps) gives +1 range to 2 STK units (the 2 Badgers). Tanker placed in North 9-10. Badgers count range from there: 3 zones to East 4 = within extended range. Backfire flies on its own at extended range (4). All legal.**Total missiles: 9 black** (Backfire 3 + Badger 3 + Badger 3)**No interception en route** (North 5-6 has Nimrod — MP doesn't intercept aircraft; North 3-4 in Bad Weather, empty). Strike is **not detected**.**CAP in East 4:** F-4 Phantom Rng 1 vs Strike (7.1.4): 3 dice A2A, Tactical +1. Modified 8+ = step loss. Natural 10 = step loss before missile launch. TF in Good Detection → strike units get **6+ save** vs CAP.**NATO CAP dice: [10, 5, 3]** (Tactical +1)- **Die 10: NATURAL 10!** Step loss before missile launch!- Die 5 (+1 = 6): Miss- Die 3 (+1 = 4): Miss**Soviet save vs CAP: 8** — SAVE! The strike unit survives!*The Sparrow missile streaks toward the lead Backfire, but the Soviet pilot breaks hard at Mach 1.4, dispensing IR flares. The missile passes within meters of the aircraft... The good detection on the convoy allows Soviet crews to anticipate the fighter positions.***All regiments intact. 9 black missiles in the air!***"LAUNCH! LAUNCH! LAUNCH!" — Nine AS-4 Kitchen and AS-5 Kelt missiles tear free from their pylons in a blaze of flame, accelerating past Mach 3 toward the wounded convoy...*All STK units and Tanker return to Kola, Spent.**SAM Defense:** US-5 (4) + Convoy (1) = 5 SAM. 9 missiles → usable SAMs = 9+2 = 11, but only 5 available → 5 SAMs.**NATO SAM dice: [10, 10, 9, 8, 3]** — EXCEPTIONAL firing!- Die 10: 2 missiles shot down- Die 10: 2 missiles shot down- Die 9: 2 missiles shot down- Die 8: 1 missile shot down- Die 3: 1 missile shot down**8 of 9 missiles shot down!** The Standard SM-1 missiles from the Spruance make an incredible showing. But **1 missile gets through.****Missile Resolution:** 1 missile, DRM +1 (Good Det). 1-2: Miss, 3-10: Hit.**Soviet resolution die: 4** (+1 = 5) → **HIT!****Allocation dice: [10, 5]** — 10 rolled! Soviet allocates → **CONVOY!**Missiles inflict 2 hits on Convoys. Convoy: 4 + 2 = **6 hits → CONVOY SUNK!***The last Kitchen strikes the heart of the merchant formation at Mach 3.5. Its 1,000 kg warhead pierces the hull of a supply tanker like paper. The detonation triggers a chain reaction — fuel tanks ignite, an ammunition ship explodes in a titanic fireball. Neighboring vessels capsize from the blast. Within minutes, a sheet of burning fuel oil covers the sea...**In Severomorsk, euphoria. Admiral Chernavin raises his vodka glass: "Za Rodinu! The capitalist convoy lies at the bottom of the Atlantic!"*---## GAME OVER### Victory Assessment**Victory Conditions:** NATO wins if the Amphib reaches Trondheim AND the Convoys reach a French port.-  Amphibious delivered to Trondheim — NATO objective fulfilled-  Convoy sunk — cannot be delivered**The Convoy can never reach a French port. NATO cannot fulfill its victory conditions.**##  SOVIET VICTORY *Admiral Chernavin rises slowly from his chair in the Severomorsk bunker. The radio operators transmit the final report to Moscow. The grave voice of the Northern Fleet Commander echoes through the room:**"Comrades... the Battle of the North Atlantic is won. The price was heavy — three submarines lost, an Alfa damaged, nine missiles to finish off a single convoy. But the capitalist supplies rest 4,000 meters below. Without those weapons and fuel, the European front will hold."**He raises his glass. "To the Fleet! To the Motherland!"*---## Final Casualty Report| Soviet Losses | NATO Losses ||---|---|| Foxtrot x2 sunk | Convoy sunk || Alfa flipped (damaged) | |## Game NotesThe NATO player deployed an excellent air defense network — the triple Phantom barrier made Soviet Bear D operations very difficult, and the SAM rolls were repeatedly outstanding (10-10-9-8-3 being the highlight). However, a single Kitchen missile from the final salvo of nine penetrated the defenses and sealed the convoy's fate. The Amphibious was successfully delivered early, demonstrating the value of swift action on the Norway track. The Soviet player struggled with early submarine losses (both Foxtrots eliminated quickly) but found success through persistent air-naval coordination — Bear D detection followed by massed Backfire/Badger strikes proved decisive.As in Tom Clancy's *Red Storm Rising*, the Battle of the Atlantic often comes down to a single missile making it through.

tier2.author: ErikLj
tier2.body: “Battles is not won by the best admiral but the one making no mistakes”, navigation pilot officer Fedotov was thinking as his Bear was slowly tumbling crippled toward the sea. Phoenix missile had shredded the whole left wing. Then he started cursing squadron navigation officer Gusjtjin and continued doing that until he met his grave in the Bay of Biscay. It had started at a routine patrol mission, “Locate the enemy convoys in the Bay och Biscay. What out for the carrier group based 400 nm west of Brest” But Gusjtin had plotted a search pattern going right over the carrier group. Nobody dared to question him. The last officer doing so was serving coffee in the briefing room. The whole squadrons had rounded the UK utilizing the gap in the air cover as the RAF were busy defending their own bases and headed for the Bay och Biscay with the radars of. Suddenly radar warning receivers were squeaking and Phoenix from Lt Michells and the other started hitting the Bears. One by one, the Bears fell burning from the sky, the whole squadron were eliminated because of a stupide navigation mistake. (2*N10 on the CAP vs MP).But then disaster struck. Backfires managed to sneak past the UK and launce swarms of missiles against the convoy just outside the ports of France. They took losses from the F14s but there were just too many missiles. Ships of all kinds were struck and went down in flames. The taskforce was almost completely eliminated. The much need supply to fight the red army in Europe was at the bottom of the Bay of Biscay. The Luftwaffe tried to make one last effort stop the second attempt to invade Denmark. They only managed to lose a couple of Tornados to some Yak36.   Denmark was now more or less without defense. Op-plan #4-9 was back on the table.To keep up the first strike capacity after the loss of some Yankees USSR decided to move some boomers from the arctic to east coast of the USA. Nato reacted in force with submarines and air assets. A few were sunk but the deterrence patrol was restored for the moment.The battle for the UK continued with more sub launce missiles and a raid by some Badgers. Some success but to the cost of a lot of Badgers. The RAF with help from USAF has learned some lessons.This is GT3 of the 1983 Tactical Surprise scenario without options played by Erik and Fredrik by Vassal. Map is start of GT4.

tier2.author: Caustizer
tier2.body: Recently I felt the urge to play this game to it's most insane level - with all the toys and rules - to see what it feels like. And yeah, it's pretty nuts. After taking a day and a half to set it up, this is what the board looks like:So what does this mean? Both sides receive a lot of toys, including ones that weren't finished historically (due to Soviet economic problems or detente) and the most advanced naval technologies at the time are now available. War has been expected for some time, so both sides have made moves to prepare meaning action heats up very quickly. But, in order to make this post more useful I'll break down some of my strategic thinking and plays made to maybe guide other players as to how they should be perceiving the game. Doing a full battle report would take way to much time and space, so maybe just the setup for now.NATO SETUP:Preamble: We have lots of Convoys available, but as a consequence the Soviet Submarines are already going to be in position to hunt them. Since the arrival of these ships intact is vital to winning the game, they will need to be as well protected as possible. The convoys already at sea are worryingly thin. Task Forces Black and Mustang are comically under guarded - we have to do something otherwise the Soviets will take those Convoy Massacre Tokens straight to the "Hammer and Sickle" bank. In addition, Castro's Cuba and Gaddafi's Libya are fully in the Soviet circle and loaded with their equipment including some nuclear weapons - this problem will need to be dealt with swiftly, especially Cuba. Additional US assets have been given to us for this purpose.1) Submarine Breakdown - YES - Adding an escorting nuclear submarine greatly increases their resilience against enemy submarine attacks. This rule allows you to break down a US Sturgeon or US Los Angeles Sub into two parts and then assign both to Task Forces at sea. You should absolutely do this, probably with the Sturgeon (Los Angeles are tougher, so better used more aggressively) since it protects your convoys. Breakdown Sturgeons added to TF Mustang and Aegis (gotta protect that French carrier, of course).US Surface Ship Breakdown - NO - I didn't break down my US ships because there are plenty of them thanks to it being '89 and Production Option. This rule is more useful in earlier years and under greater surprise when your escorts are spread thin and need to be distributed more evenly between Task Forces.2) Ship Units Moved - YES - I moved two of the Ticonderoga VLS ships and US-11, US-12 to Task Forces Mustang and Black to buff up their protection. Multiple T VLS ships in one Task force have a diminishing return, so spreading their protective and offensive missiles out makes a lot of sense.3) Task Force Formed - YES - This one was a toss up between forming a TF with the pre-positioned US Carriers & Fleet in Spain, and the UK Fleet in the UK. I chose the US Fleet because I know I don't have the production points to upgrade the UK Carrier to the Elizabeth (sob!) so this is the best way to get carriers to the GUIK line quickly.4) Submarine Units placed on the Map - YES - many players will look at this and think "great, I can teleport my best subs into the North Sea and just clobber whatever the Soviets send" but this is the wrong way to do it, in my opinion. It might take some time, but your best nuclear subs will arrive there fairly quickly within a day or two. The best use for these 7 free moves is to preposition the abundance of Slow, Diesel Submarines NATO has in Europe with high attack values on the ocean in locations where they are going to be most effective. That way, they can just attack and not bother with moving. Hence, the Soviets have to deal with them as opposed to just ignoring them as usual. With this many pre-positions though the SOSUS guard duties can't be ignored though, so I split the difference. Two Kobbens, the Delphin and the Daphne are placed in the North Sea, Baltic Sea and Barents Sea to strike at any incoming Soviet Task Forces that enter their zone. Three Los Angeles are placed next to the GUIK line to guard it (see why I didn't break one down?).5) Air Units on Patrol - YES - With these I've setup localized patrols in the North Sea, Baltic Sea and Barents Sea plus one off the coast of Cuba to deter Soviet anti-submarine strikes (since they now have Production - Helicopters there). I could've assigned MP units, but it doesn't make much sense to do that - I don't know what the weather is going to be and the Soviet submarines will just avoid the patrols or have magnetic hulls.6) Carrier Move - YES - I moved a carrier to task force Mustang to further beef it up. No point in having three US carriers in one task force when there's lots of work to be done across the board. Not to mention the fact the Soviets start 1 First Strike Point away from Nukes at sea which is the mortal enemy of US carrier stacking.7) Production - ABSOLUTELY YES - So with 8 points of bonus production, there are a lot of choices. I know I have Reinforced Iceland already, so Patriot Missiles might seem a bit much but I know the Soviets will come on hard so I spend 2 to buy them for Germany and the UK. 2 more on another Los Angeles sub, because they are the best subs in the game, and 4 points on US-12 to get a heavy escort for my double convoy coming up first turn.Soviet Setup:Preamble: As the attacker, the pressure is on us to undermine NATO and defeat them before the end of the game. This is not an easy task. We need to gather at least 4 "Hammer and Sickles", which are gained through Convoy Massacres, Successes on Land (which tend to follow said massacres), and winning the war of nuclear posturing by gaining lots of "First Strike Points" but not spending them on nuking your enemies. How nuclear the game is to become is totally in the hands of the Soviet player, and we need to get our Subs in position to gain a lot of these points but also be careful about using them - if we spend them to stop NATO from nuking us in return (in the process forfeiting the advantages they give our ships and soldiers) it will pay dividends when the inevitable first exchange occurs. If it's just demonstration strikes and not full apocalypse, we win. But enough of this grand thinking - what should we actually do to achieve this?1) Soviet Technology - YES, BUT HOLD YOUR HORSES COMRADE - You can permanently spend Soviet Spies to upgrade your units with valuable tech, but since Spies are one of your best assets every one your lose hurts. My advice is pick a game plan, pick ONE technology to maximize that plan, and then carry on. I chose to upgrade my Torpedoes since I'm gonna bank hard on the Submarines.2) Take a Backfire to replace Badgers - NO - This is pointless in 89 since you get the Backfire anyway. Just add to Kola and move on.3) Move Strike Units - YES, BUT - There's minimal action in the Mediterranean normally, unless you have Libya. I moved the Strike in Syria to the Baltic where it will be more useful. NATO has Patriots so casualties will be high amongst Strike planes and we'll need all we can get.4) Move Surface Units - YES - Again, I shifted units in Syria to the Baltic. Landings in this game are a case of "red-rover" where whichever tools you bring in the task force can cancel enemy dice effects. The Moskava and Kresta ships are better used in the Baltic TF then doing nyet in the Med.5) Move Submarines to Sea - ABSOLUTELY YES - Getting the chance to move like 18 submarines to sea is huge. I grabbed all the Diesel subs in Kola and peppered them throughout the Atlantic to light up any NATO convoys trying to cross. This no-brainer move saves them many turns and OPs of moving there on their own (not to mention trying to get past GUIK, ugh!). The remaining assignments are used to pair up the nuke subs in the Bastion to prepare for GUIK passage and assign Alfa Subs to the North Sea - NATO has a really hard time dealing with them!6) Create Two Task Forces - YES - One off Kola to invade Norway (or Iceland) and one off Leningrad to invade Germany. Done. Saves you the OPs of doing it yourself.7) Weather = no control over this at all. Same with Tattletales. RORSATS = cover the NATO convoy and amphib turn-in points. as many of them as you can. this gives you "last shot" opportunities at them before they reach their destination.8) Soviet Production - YES YES YES - Time to have some fun. Since I've boosted my nuclear submarines with tech, naturally I'll buy better SAMs (to protect my main bases and Cuba) along with two more Alfas, Helicopters in Cuba and a Victor.9) Cuba and Libya Active - MORE FUN - So technically I can move all Soviet surface ships to Cuba thanks to this option. Is it a good idea? Absolutely not. But you can do it. They'd have nothing to do apart from die to overwhelming US firepower with no landing destinations, but hey do you remember Red Dawn? What about Red Alert 2? The reality is, you should assign some dated Strike planes and May MP to Libya to tickle NATO there and move two nuke sub pairs (with escorts) from the Bastion and Kola into Cuba. Why? Because now instead of having 8 points of nukes down there now you have 16. If the NATO player doesn't deal with these four pairs, the Soviet player will have the nuclear initiative which isn't good. The Yankee subs aren't worth much to the US player anymore, so expect your Deltas to be targeted which is fine. It gives you more time to win the war in Europe. It gives them something to do as opposed to near-suicidally charging the GUIK line.I hope you enjoyed this analysis. Might post the first moves on this game soon.Cheers.

tier2.threadTitle: Questions as I work through a long-range air strike.

tier2.author: Rick
tier2.body: 1. Correct - they need to fly to a sea zone bordering the UK airbase and launch from there. The long-range here is in contrast to NATO bombing. Essentially while you'll use aircraft to carry them, what you will ultimately execute is a cruise missile attack, which is significant for things like how SAM counters respond, what would happen if the strike was escorted, exact table rolled on for the attack etc. The only missiles with multi-zone range are green land attack ones, and assuming you're playing 83 without options there are none of those around. 2. Sadly, tankers can only assist Strike aircraft - not fighters or MP. From memory I think that was an errata point. This means your strike will be unescorted, but as consolation you will get a 6+ save against losses inflicted by the CAP.3. Ships in port wouldn't be relevant even if the port was attacked - ship SAM are for self defence. Note that your salvo of missiles will become a 1-3 dice attack - check the cruise missiles vs land chart.4 &5. Assuming there's one in position (presumably at least the RAF fighters) then yes. Note CAP from a damaged base takes a penalty. Saratoga could do the CAP instead (and probably should)*IF* it is in the specifc sea zone the strike fires from.5. You would, but as previously noted it sadly can't get there!Finally as a tactical note - I would be very reluctant to have the Bear-G attack any kind of target that can shoot back at it. It's a unique capability (6 range, potentially 8 with a tanker!) Which coupled with the Arctic overflight arrows means it can happily throw missiles at anything in the Atlantic. It is also not that tough, and it sucks when it dies. If the UK bases are damaged any fighters out on patrol are forced back spent, which means the direct route from the Kola should be open. tier2.body: My experiences in a first attempt at a campaign game using 1983 tactical surprise.First, I grabbed a pdf version of both sets of rules (the original with errata and the alternate rules layout version 1.05)  As of the beginning of Day 15: WP currently has taken Oslo, Turkey, sunk 2 US carriers and occupied Kiel.   The only thing preventing a WP victory is task force Black in Med 1-2 pounding the southern track to prevent the capture of Rome.  Unfortunately for NATO, WP forces have 3 units that can take Denmark in the next two days (1 turn.)   The nearest help is mid 8-9 where on US CV is currently part of a slow transport TF scheduled to take troops to Iceland.  The loss of two US carriers was a consequence of placing insufficient anti-air support with the task forces.   Someone posted some WP guidelines on strategy and there was a suggestion not to ‘piss away’ strike aircraft.  Thus, the WP attacked with the goal of being able to get 12 missile points available to launch at a force.  The Tomcats were not as effective as I anticipated as I forgot that unless you roll a natural 10, odds are, the missiles are going to launch (I may have not been using the critical hit process properly, but aside from the two sunk US carriers, a third was damaged and repaired; the French also lost their carrier.)WP collected FSP’s by risking its SSBNS and used the points to reconstitute depleted air units.  WP was somewhat successful in protecting its first strike units by using its spy network to prevent the successful location and attack of SSBN’s.  Over time, however, the spy network was eliminated, and NATO’s successful effort led to the state of ‘Nuclear Fear.’  I’m sure I’ve made a ton of mistakes; I only hope there were evenly distributed between both sides.  (My initial confusion on the location of the Kiel/Schleswig/Esbjerg complex and when Danish fighters were employed, for example, may have led to delays in striking both that complex and the eastern Baltic complex of the WP.   if anyone has picked up play errors in this short narrative, I welcome the feedback.I was going to call the game, but I think NATO may be able to pull this off if one TF (currently in MED) can move and stop progress in the Denmark track, while the second CVBG force sheds its amphibious unit and races to Med to continue to hold off progress on the southern track.

tier2.author: felixh
tier2.body: According to 16.2.2, as one action, multiple submarines may move into one zone and then make a combined missile attack.How should this action be executed/sequenced in the face of possible On Patrol interruptions?My interpretation is this:Active player declares Missile Coordination action and specifies all participating submarines and the destination zone, and spends Ops. No Ops refunds, regardless of what happens next.Then active player chooses one sub at a time to move to destination (if not already there). As each moves, it may be intercepted by On Patrol units in the usual way. All chosen subs must attempt to move to the destination, even if they, or others, take losses. After all surviving subs reach the destination, the active player can choose to abandon the missile attack.All subs initially chosen are marked Spent, even if they didn't move or attack.Does this make sense?Another approach would be to let the active player react to hits on moving subs by stopping movement early for that sub, maybe extending to abandoning the move of subs that haven't moved yet. I'd still force the active player to pay the originally computed Ops points.-Felix

tier2.author: illusionDS
tier2.body: Chris L  @chris196775 3. CAP : when a raid (escorted strike) attacks a facility or TF that does not have a CAP, but when there is another TF with a CAP that may defend the target.(for example : strike attack on a facility that has no CAP but there is a TF with CAP near the facility ; or strike attack on a TF without CAP but there is another TF with CAP in the sea zone)- This is my main question : does the CAP, which is not attached to the the target, but is able to defend it, have to combat (and being spent if not) or can the player choose to not react to the raidThere are various erratas regarding CAP, and confusions over "facilities" and "land areas" (strikes should target Land Areas, not Facilities, you only allocate attack dice to *eligible* facilities after rolling CAP, SEAD, and SAM).For what Land Areas are, read this: https://boardgamegeek.com/thread/2685341/article/38217774#38...For your first example, "escorted strike attack on a facility that has no CAP but there is a TF with CAP near the facility", errata says that only carrier CAP in the same zone as the strike aircraft can participate in combat against it. If the strike is escorted (which results in fighter vs fighter combat), either side's fighter can choose to disengage and be spent.For your second example, "escorted strike attack on a TF without CAP but there is another TF with CAP in the sea zone", again results in fighter vs fighter combat, so again either side can disengage and be spent.Also, remember that land-based CAP cannot choose to disengage since they're not considered to be "in a sea zone"https://boardgamegeek.com/thread/2719405/can-landbased-cap-a...
