tier2.author: Nicolas
tier2.body: Stuart Tonge  @stuuk Tons of math I had to dig around in my notes but I found the details:1 x Clem/Foch -> Capital (only one because the other is in refit)1 x Aconit (but a single unit) **1 x Cassard (1989) **6 x Commandant Riviere  @3 x George Leygues (Crotale)1 x Suffren **2 x Tourville **11 x D'estienne D'Orves @The double stars are the mixed unit, so it's all the good stuff really:1 x Aconit (but a single unit) **1 x Cassard (1989) **1 x Suffren **2 x Tourville **4 hulls (5 in 1989) at a readiness of 66% (which is the number I used) is only 3 ships, so i actually gave it a bump and added in some George Leygues to make up the numbers with crotale rated (generously) as somewhat effective - which is shall we say.. dubious against something like an AS-4!Unfortunately, the @ ships don't have any SAM capability and only serve to carry Exocet equivalents, so in the scope of the game they are pretty much just targets, as such, i missed them out or assumed they were there but just didn't have very much effect - they were a large part of the overall surface force.You are right about Jean d'arc though, that could have been an extra helo carrier.Overall the French navy IS underrepresented.. but, it just wasn't very effective in the time period of the game (that's not a slight to the no-doubt very brave & effective seamen, rather that their equipment was old and not designed for this scale of conflict).The best French assets are the ones you never see - the nuke boats, and the hunter killers, which are very good - as well as the diesels.Oh, I'm not saying the French navy was great - just that it was bigger ...A few points  points: - the "@" ships were not only MM38 carriers, but ASW escorts, so that may well have resulted in an increased ASW value compared to the "1" we have (there are a lot of them, and they were designed for long range patrols);- speaking of hunter-killers, you could add a one-step unit of Rubis in 85.  That would give the carrier group a "national" escort - you'd probably need a French fighter unit at Toulon - there are several air bases in the area that would have flown CAP over the area (with relatively modern F1C's).The one thing that is a bit more problematic is the classification of Brest as a convoy port - it couldn't really.  I'm house ruling that convoys landing there get +1 hit (infrastructure is inadequate).  And "Cherbourg" is really Le Havre, but that's cosmetic.But the game is very good !  (just stated a 1985 campaign on Vassal).

Maybe to of a liberal interpretation but that's how I solve it. Thus, to me multiple spy usage and NATO Boomer Hunt rolls are fine as long you have the means (fortunate die roll and enough spies) to do it. When NATO uses nuclear weapons one does not use the Nuclear markers but the War marker is pushed back from Ruhr to Münster/Frankfurt as written in 20.0.

tier2.author: LeSpass
tier2.body: Quote:Hmm I'm not sure how that would help you?It would help to cancel a hit on the Task Force as per the bullet point 9 from 17.11 of the rulebook. “For each roll of 8 or higher, the Task Force owner may select and remove one of the already rolled attacking submarines dice from those rolled in step 2, thus preventing the hit from taking place.”With the ‘Determined attack’ event ignoring natural 8, 9 and 10, the roll of 7 plus 1 Tactical value modifier is the only way to avoid a hit on bad weather when that event is played. (rocket torpedoes cannot be used on bad weather as per the point 7 from 17.11 of the rulebook)

tier2.author: Rick
tier2.body: A few weekends ago I got a chance to play through the full campaign in one sitting, after a few runs through on Vassal.I played NATO in the 1985 Tactical Surprise scenario with Options. I got Decoys for Convoys; my opponent burned two spies to take White Sea Bastion, Turkish Neutrality, and Production.Our game ended in a decisive NATO win by Internal Coup in Turn 6. This was my first time playing in 85 and with Options, and I had a few realisations which might be useful to those making the jump!85 change - Green missilesNot many to go round, but a surprisingly impactful shift in strategy. My experience in the '83 runs had taught me to put a very high value on anything that let me kill enemy units without them getting to shoot back. Combat in BWN is usually attritional - consider a sub attacking a convoy, or (another) bombing raid hitting the UK. The Yankee Notch in the Kola should be firing every other turn - with range 2 it can hit the UK, Iceland - even Brest or Kiel, all from the Barents Sea. I got lucky and killed it when it first emerged - because my opponent didn't have a sacrificial 8 survivability sub lurking to soak up hits.Conversely, I struck Cuba for the first time ever this game, which was very useful in shutting down the Cuba Bear-D and a couple of RORSATS. I'd previously run the maths and concluded that to do it reliably without Tomahawk requires carrier support. In my assessment the carriers are needed in too many other places, and the air wings too valuable to risk getting shot down by a lucky Cuban Mig-21. Add in a salvo of 3 Tomahawk before the bombers, however, and it's a different game entirely. I didn't try them versus the main Soviet bases (my opponent was running upgraded SAMs, and I wasn't willing to give away any FSP by striking the Kola) but I suspect they would have made a significant difference there as well.85 change - 2nd Bear-GOr as I dubbed it - Satan's Own Bats. This single unit was probably the biggest shift between 83 and 85. In 83, my standard package for task forces was a single escort unit per convoy/amph, plus a sub. That usually creates a task force with an ASW value of about 12, and about 3 SAMs. I'd found that struck the right balance between giving my opponent lots of targets to pick up with limited detection assets, and the targets being hard enough that they wouldn't immediately keel over.Assuming the TF is out in the Mid-Atlantic and you're manning the GIUK line, the Bear-G are the only unit capable of reaching your TF without interception. In 83, that means a 6 missile salvo. After SAMs, that's probably 2 hits - painful, but survivable. in 85, there can very easily be 12 missiles inbound - probably about 6 hits, which wrecks the escort and the convoy in one strike. I lost multiple convoys to this before ultimately withdrawing them all under the screen of the late arriving carriers. Had I not aggressively prosecuted the boomers to force an early end, I would have been in significant difficulty in Germany before too long.OptionsMy opponent spent 2 spies on options, and another on air to air missiles. Noting that weakness, I hammered the Yankees early on, and had sunk them all by Turn 3. He felt after the fact that his Options hadn't been worth it - they look cool, but the spies were more valuable. I deliberately didn't give him any FSP to use instead, and some of the Options he got worried me quite a lot in the planning - but in the end, I agree with him.Decoys - not very interesting, basic utility option. My opponent wound up principally using air to target the convoys so it didn't see much use. Nice to have, not a game changer.Turkish Neutrality - loss of Turkish units is only a minor inconvenience as the Soviets usually struggle in the Med. I've never ever seen the Turkish overflight fighters used! The only impact was the free shift on the Europe South track; between light Soviet opposition and reasonably fortunate dice from me, they never made it out of Trieste.Production - made him a bit better in various ways, but didn't really present any new threat for me to manage. He did take the additional tanker and one of the Flankers; I would have taken the other Flanker instead of the upgraded SAMs. Only the Flankers really worried me, and they scored a mutual kill against some patrolling Tornado ADV in the first UK strike of the game. That significantly complicated my defence of the UK airbases; had he taken both, he could probably have also swept out some of the Icelandic fighters.White Sea Bastion - looked very worrying, but actually turned out to be a White Elephant. My experience from 83 was that the trade between the bastion and going under the ice was about survivability. They're actually much more survivable under the ice, but it's nearly impossible to kill the Los Angeles that will be hunting them. In contrast, a Los Angeles attacking the bastion would quite often score some kills on its way in, but would then be hunted down itself. Moving to the White Sea only amplified that change, with the additional +1 to hit for both sides and the lack of hydrophones. The subtler impacts came from the Second Strike card being disabled, and from the Bastion now being at range zero from the Barents Sea. That means that subs manning the SOSUS line can go straight from there to attacking into the bastion, extending the "potential threats" range out another zone. tier2.author: TFGA73
tier2.body: BWN has a learning curve because it operates much differently than a lot of other war games.  For example, the concept that you have to detect surface units before attacking but not submarines throws off a lot of people at first.  Another example is the planes with a range of ‘0’, which I eventually figured out means they can only protect their base.   It also mixes in a fair amount of abstraction, and understanding how that blends into the crunchier parts takes a little time.  In my opinion the time investment is worth it.  This is one of the top three games I’ve ever played.   The different strategies, the random events, and how close both sides are to the edge of disaster the entire time make it very replayable.  If I ever sold off my game collection and could only keep one, this would be it.

tier2.author: oakleaf
tier2.body: I love this game and have played many full games.There are IMHO two aspects of the game that I think have triggered so much activity on this board.The first is that the rulebook is very condensed.  That is, all the rules are in there but they are very rarely repeated or cross referenced so it can sometimes be frustrating to find the exact combination of situations that applies and piece it all together.  This becomes less of an issue through play because the base rules become automatic and you're only dealing with the exceptions.The second is that the cards can throw wrinkles in that are not always directly resolved in the rules.  This is pretty typical where games have cards.  It is slightly exacerbated here because the systems are tightly linked and cards (both event and reaction) can be played at many times during the turn so some really difficult situations can arise.I believe this game has a lot going for it and I strongly recommend it.  But, you will need to really get to know the rulebook.

tier2.body: So MPs can fly and attack, fly and detect TF, or fly and go on patrol.Assuming FTRs are present and eligible to react, it sounds like from reading the rule book, PAC and errata together, that you add tactical value to die roll to get modified result, but modified result only determines whether MP is disrupted or not.Disruptions cause MPs that fly and attack (i.e., ASW) or fly and go on patrol to return to base spent. So if the MP have 2 search die and receive 1 disruption, they can still search with 1 die before returning to base spent.  I assume that's not the case with ASW.The modified die roll does not cause a step loss, ever.  Only natural rolls cause step losses against MPs (N10 vs plane, N8-10 vs helo).The phrase "Die roll + Tactical Value = kills allowed" is a typo then that neither belongs on Fighter Combat vs. Maritime Patrol (MP) PAC or in rule book under 17.5.If so, then I think the errata needs to make that more clear.  If I'm understanding correctly, the phrase never applies against MPs.I agree with Pablo, it needs to be made clear the phrase shouldn't be there as it never applies.  The errata only explains disruption results vs MP performing attacks or going on patrol, and not searching.

tier2.body: Dear all,I have just received my physical copy and have started unpunching the counters - and going through the rules and cards.I do have a few questions regarding ports:- Rule 13.2 references a delivery to "any Belgian port" to get a bonus (eg treat a 5-hit convoy as partial supply).  Problem: there is only one (Antwerp), Amsterdam (which should really be Rotterdam, a much bigger harbor complex than Amsterdam) is in the Netherlands, not Belgium.  I am assuming the rule applies to both.  If not, what is the rationale, and why mention Belgian portS plural?- for French ports, "Cherbourg" is misplaced, the port depicted by the port icon is Le Havre (France's largest port), Cherbourg is at the tip of the Cotentin peninsula and is a naval base, not a commercial port (it would have trouble handling the traffic).  This is purely cosmetic because they are both in the same sea zone.  However, having Brest (a major military port) as a convoy port is a bit more problematic as, like Cherbourg, it has nowhere near the infrastructure needed to unload 40+ freighters full of military equipment and get the supplies / troops on the way and to the front within a reasonable time (being at the tip of Britanny adds a healthy 591 kms of driving for a truck just to reach Paris....).  Yet, it is easier to reach than Le Havre (one sea zone).  In France, only Le Havre and Marseille / La Ciotat have that kind of capacity (Toulon is purely a naval base, but, again, this is cosmetic as Marseille & Toulon are in the same sea zone).  House rule proposal: either treat Le Havre as a "Belgian" port (it is also very well connected to the northern European road/rail/river freight network) or treat convoys unloading in Brest as having an extra hit: the convoys would need to split between a few smaller ports in Brittany, like Saint Malo, Lorient, Saint Nazaire, and the road/rail network is not as dense there as it is around Paris.- for Italian ports, I wonder why the bonus is given to Taranto, which, like Brest, is pretty far from the front and is not a major commercial port, as opposed to La Spezia / Genoa, which does have the proper infrastructure and is in Northern Italy, where the action is.Talking about ports: you should also add a nuclear trigger right before Toulon is captured: the French were pretty keen about the "sanctuarization" of their territory and would not have stood idle as Pact forces crossed the border there.Incidentally, I really like the idea underpinning the unloading rules - just my failed-geography-professor-side showing up again!

tier2.author: TFGA73
tier2.body: So I just wrapped up a solo game of BWN, taking place in 1989 with Tactical Surprise in effect.   I always play using the options events, and in this case the Soviets had a very strong draw, pulling Production (I.e., extra units), the Arab-Israeli conflict and the SSBN focus.   The Middle East option placed a lot of strain on NATO, but they pulled it out, and they also held their own in the north, dragging out the Norway offensive and hanging on in Denmark.   The problem was the boomers; the SSBN option allows the extra boomers to start in first strike zones, and the Delta IV joined the Yankees on station.   Try as they might, the NATO subs just couldn’t catch them.   Evasions, saves by the Delta IV, spies not getting caught, lucky card draws, and terrible rolls by sub after sub.   Not until turn 6 did NATO finally start knocking out a couple.  This allowed the Russians to pile up a ridiculous amount of FSPs, and on turn 7 they played the Battlefield Nuke rule and stormed the Ruhr, and topped that a turn later by taking Antwerp (oh yeah, NATO’s convoy protection wasn’t too hot either—all that boomer chasing opened up holes in the ASW net). Facing certain loss, NATO went for the Hail Mary and tried to force a coup by attacking the Soviet boomer bastion.  Of course now NATO gets the hot dice and drops several deltas and the Typhoon in short order.  This triggered the “Politburo Intervenes”spot on the Soviets stability track, putting the Nuclear Strike card in-hand, and here I realized I made an epic mistake.   Never having had a game get to this point and not reading the card previously, I thought the Soviet nuclear strike was triggered by nukes at sea, not battlefield nukes.   Uh-oh.    So the Soviets do what any rational totalitarian regime does and plays the card, and rolls a 3.  Armageddon (“Strategic Exchange” as the card put it). Whoops.  Note to self:   Once the Russians trigger nukes, leave the bastion alone. . .

tier2.author: Brastias
tier2.body: Perhaps an abbreviated version of the 17.11 combat sequence could be useful to answer a couple of your questions:1) The submarine player announces the target Task Force2) The submarine player rolls the dice and determines whether any hits have been scored3) If there are no hits, the combat ends now4) If the submarine rolled a double (a pair) then it may conduct an SSM (missile) attack5) Calculate the Task Force ASW6) Look-up the ASW total to determine the number of dice to be rolled7) If the Task Force rolled a double it may alter one of the dice to an 8 and discard the other die8) For each die, check to see if the roll plus Tactical Value is enough to cause a step loss on the attacking submarine9) For each roll of 8 or higher, the Task Force owner may  remove one of the already rolled attacking submarines dice from those rolled in step 2.10) Evaluate the remaining submarine attack dice.A1. You attack one TF only so any SSM's would attack the same force.A2. The hits in step 4, unlike other hits, are implemented immediately, which is why those two dice are removed.A3. tier2.author: Abe
tier2.body: ALAN CARLSON  @PScipio Supposedly, the excess Essex-class CV were to play the CVE role as CVSs. Oops, out of money (thanks Vietnam)!Maybe, but I think their wartime role was supposed to be strategic ASW; i.e., hunting down the Soviet SSBNs that had to deploy to the Western Atlantic and Eastern Pacific because of short-ranged SLBMs. When the Soviets got longer-range SLBMs and could operate either closer to their home or disappear into vaster stretches of ocean, this mission became less important and so the main rationale for preserving this capability went away.Whether the Soviets were actually planning to make a significant effort attacking Allied shipping is an interesting question. It would seem axiomatic that they would want to do so in order to support their ground offensive, and that is how most WWIII fiction and games approach the issue. Tom Clancy's novel Red Storm Rising is almost entirely about this problem and it's what drives a lot of the action in our games including this one. But the Soviets weren't planning to win WWIII in a few weeks; they were planning to win it in a few days. With that kind of timeframe, the Atlantic pipeline is largely irrelevant: either the Soviets reach the Rhine and beyond or they don't, opposed almost entirely by NATO's "at start" forces and whatever can be mobilized and flown over quickly. In that case, the Soviets would probably be focusing on strategic ASW (protecting their own boomers and hunting ours) and neutralizing the USN as an offensive force.

tier2.body: Alan, check this out:https://www.thedrive.com/the-war-zone/39809/the-navy-experim..."On June 7th, 1971, the USS Saratoga (CVA-60), along with her escorts and support ships, first made their way into the North Atlantic before turning south and then east into the Mediterranean Sea for what would be a very odd and special deployment – a four-month experiment that would test a new concept in ASW and introduce a remodeled way of thinking about what “aircraft carrier” could mean to the United States Navy. It turns out, these tests may very well have been decades ahead of their time......The “attack carrier,” or CVA, would embark the fleet’s fighter and attack aircraft, while the “anti-submarine carrier,” or CVS, would continue the much-loved hunter-killer concept and embark both fixed-wing and rotary-wing ASW aircraft."...Perhaps history does repeat itself. These new distributed ASW ideas are strikingly similar to those tested aboard the Sara 50 years ago. Since there is no long-range ASW aircraft currently flying from our aircraft carrier decks and if we’re not going to introduce an ASW version of the MV-22 Osprey (which we should seriously reconsider), then maybe it’s time to go back to the future and have TACAIR do ASW once again.Damm! Hopefully a war planner will try BWN and think "wouldn't it be cool if I had a CV based ASW force to protect those convoys for Europe?". Probably not; they'll be fantasying about being Tom Cruise The CVS home rule and counter in BWN is born

tier2.author: PScipio
tier2.body: The US Navy has been terrible at protecting the US Merchant Marine since ... 1775.  Their worst showing was the US Civil War, when a handful of Confederate raiders swept the seas - until that point, the American merchant fleet was larger than the British. The less said about USN protection off the US East Coast and (worse) Trindidad in 1942, the better.  In the Cold War, the USN dusted off the HUK (Hunter-Killer) concept that worked fine against WWII subs without snorkels - when you had Ultra to tell you where they were. Meanwhile, Liberty ships were cheap and plentiful, and  you could teach a high school graduate from southern Minnesota how to run it. Supposedly, the excess Essex-class CV were to play the CVE role as CVSs. Oops, out of money (thanks Vietnam)! [I'm biased - my dad graduated from Fairmont (MN) high in June 1942, joined the US Merchant Marine in August, and after training as a radio officer, set sail in July 1943 to the UK, Italy, and Okinawa. Per capita losses among American merchant mariners were higher than in any US armed services, and they never got the recognition FDR promised them.]I think it is great that BWN puts the merchant convoys front and center - the idea that REFORGER would work with nothing but aircraft was fanciful.

tier2.author: Herr
tier2.body: Our third turn – Day 5 & 6 – in the 1983 Campaign…We began playing Blue Water Navy: The War at Sea in FEB. We selected the 1983 Cold War Goes Hot Campaign Game. Fantastic fun and storyline only a meaty, complex wargame beast can deliver. And, BWN is delivering in spades. As an aside, I compared BWN to a couple of similarly rated, HEAVY weight (game weight) games published relatively recently to see how it stacked up:...and it compares quite favorably: check out that game lust rating!Previous session reports covering the first four days of the conflict here:Session Two:  Session One:  To recap the action to date: * SOVIETs scrambled their boomer fleet to off the coast of Iceland (via the Arctic)* SOVIETs encountered a Sea of Sorrows (aka North Sea): many sunk, noisy subs.* Action in Norway. RED tanks roll, but are pummeled. Same story in Southern Europe. However, Premier JRs boys were making good progress in Northern Europe.* NATO was able to sink a few boomers, triggering a box slide in Soviet political stability.* NATO attempting to rush supplies and troops to Europe* Overall edge to NATO, but, we're only in the early innings.And, we're having a TON OF FUN. Completely enjoying the game.Before we jump into session three, a few additional thoughts on the mechanics of the game...Progress on the War Tracks, First Strike Points and Soviet StabilityClueless: So, when we began, we clearly had no idea what the hell we were doing. This is ALWAYS the case with a meaty, complex operational strategic wargame. I think it took me 20 to 30 plays with Paths of Glory until I thought “I get it”. Then, I played Pete Reese at WBC in PoG tourney. After a few turns, he said, “So, do you have an actual plan to win this game?”. Pete proceeded to destroy me in a 6 turns. Then, I had to play some more. Back to Blue Water Navy.So what are you solving for? Soviets win by gaining “Hammer and Sickle” points. Most of these seem to be on the War Tracks. As the Soviet tanks roll one space a turn on each track towards victory, NATO must slow down their progress. Generally, this occurs by bombing some of the tracks, delivering supplies to a track (a front) or sending troops. In each of those cases, NATO has to use its naval assets to deliver the appropriate payload. The Soviets attempt to thwart that. So the dance involves NATO pushing naval assets towards Europe and the REDs attempting to send them to bottom of the Atlantic and Med (which also generate Hammer and Sickle points from convoy massacres and sunk USA carriers {the horror!}. . And there is another couple of “tensions”…First Strike Points and Soviet Stability Track. Soviets get these buggers (FSPs) primarily from stationing boomers close to the USA. FSPs can be used to exert pressure on NATO in a variety of ways. The trade off is that the Soviets expose their boomers. Sunk boomers trigger rolls on the Soviet Stability table. The Soviets want to REALLY avoid these rolls. Why? As the Soviet Stability Track moves to the right, Soviet options are crimped. If a internal coup occurs, the game ends. If the game ends prior to the REDs racking up enough Hammer and Sickle points, the promise of a workers paradise will be deferred until next false prophet/ideology or charlatan arrives on the scene (happens every few decades, so, no great loss).I think we were finally beginning to understand how things worked together when we began Turn 3. Of course, we had both committed significant errors by then, but, we were having a blast and wanted to delve deeper into the game to better understand how things fit together. We continued on the day before May Day 2021…Turn 3: Day 5: A Bloodied NATO Nose, but a slide towards a Soviet CoupTurn begins with Soviets tossing down a “9 Ops” card and NATO responding with 15 Ops.Premier JRT3D5 Start CardsT3D5S1 (Turn 3, Day 5, Soviet Impulse 1): Premier JR launches a ROSAT – the first of many. Soviets were desperately trying to locate NATO TFs (Task Forces) to prevent any further interference with their European offensive. T3D5N1: NATO decided to pursue the Soviet wolfpack by Iceland with 3unrelenting vigor. Orion from Iceland went hunting for subs in East 9-10 (E9-10). Dice rolled. 3 hits! Althougth the Soviet player whipped out another silly save card (negates 1 hit), 2 subs took a pounding, including a Delta boomer costing the commie’s another 3 point boomer loss. NATO player smiled as the next boomer loss would cause another Soviet Stability check.T3D5N1 Hits on a WolfpackT3D5S2: Another soviet bird is launched to put eyes on the NATO TFs.T3D5N2: NATO dispatches a Nimrod from the UK that promptly puts a hit on a Victor sub in E9-10.T3D5N2 Nimrod hits a VictorT3D5S3: Another soviet bird in the air targets N5-6. A comment here. NATO player was holding a card that would stop ROSAT launched this turn and limit to 1 next turn, but, did not think granting the SOVIETs one First Strike Point would be worth the exchange. FSPs seem to be the currency the SOVIETs desperately need. So, even though NATO TFs would likely be detected as a result, and possible losses would ensue, NATO could not see under what conditions it would ever allow the SOVIETs to gain a FSP.Back to the SOVIET play. So, the bird detects a NATO TF. NATO player snickered and tossed a card that invalidated the detection. Premier JR shouted, “You’re a d*ck”. I love wargames: no silly Eurogame balanced fairness exist. Dice/card gods don’t like you? Tough: life’s cruel. Of course, I can whine about poor luck with the best of them.T3D5N3: NATO dispatches another sub to the front via M6-7.T3D5S3 TF Hammer avoids detectionT3D5S4: SOVIET continued its pursuit to find NATO TFs. This time success in with good detection on TF Aegis.T3D5N4: Orion dispatched to E3 for sub hunting. A fail.T3D5N4 hunting in E3 for RED subsT3D5S5:SOVIET decides to reap some of the rewards of detecting NATO TFs.  TF Aegis drew the short lot. A SOVIET Victor sub attacked and placed three hits on the TF. NATO was able to play a card to nullify one. When the smoked cleared, a NATO convoy ended up heavily damaged. T3D5S5 attack on TF AEGIST3D5S5 Soviets hit ConvoyT3D5N5: NATO kept up the pressure on the SOVIET boomer by hunting in W2-3. Sneaky boomer and escort successfully evaded.SOVIET STABILITY SLIPs: Allies WaiverT3D5S6: SOVIETS made a poor detection on another NATO TF: TF Hammer.T3D5N6: NATO hunted the sneaky boomer that had evaded to W4-5. Success this time. Boomer hit and a SOVIET stability roll pushes the SOVIET STABILITY TRACK to “Allies Withdraw” allowing NATO to place a partial convoy on the front of its choosing. NATO choose Northern Europe; the one front where the REDs where on the move.T3D5N6 SOVIET STABILY SLIPS AFTER BOOMER SUNKT3D5S7: Another SOVIET detection on a NATO TF: TF Hammer goes naked and the SOVIETs place a good detection marker.T3D5N7: A NATO Sturgeon places a hit on another RED sub in E9-10. NATO’s impulse triggered a FAST TF move. NATO pushed its naval assets forward. TF Hammer boldly jumped into the North Sea hoping to further blunt any RED aggression in Norway.T3D5S8: SOVIETs chose to punish NATO aggression and targeted TF Hammer in the North Sea (which had been JR’s Sea of Soviet Sorrows on Turn 1). A wounded sub attacked and placed a hit on the TF. However, the crew became hero’s of the motherland as their sub was destroyed.T3D5N8: NATO forms a TF at Norfolk with its impressive Turn 3 reinforcementT3D5S9: Sensing a wounded deer, SOVIETs again attacked TF Hammer that was aggressively positioned in the North Sea. A quick aside…A key to preventing a RED victory is to block soviet army movement on the war tracks. This can be done by some combination of bombing the associated front and delivering supplies or troops. I put together a playaid to keep track of which fronts can receive supplies and which demand troops from which ports – and which fronts can be bombed (see below). Playaid: The War Tracks...bombing, delivering supplies and troopsAs NATO, I think you’ve got to take risks with a few carriers to deliver air strikes to Norway and Southern Europe. Carriers (and their air wings) don’t provide any cover for convoys and amphibs. What up?A hole in carrier ASW assets…S3 Viking: Carrier based ASW back in the day. Sadly, seemingly absent here - wish there was a ASW CarrierYou’d think maybe NATO war planners would have developed a number of carriers with ASW based on them for just this task. I actually did a little research on the subject. The navy used S2 and S3s (P3s require a longer strip than a carrier flattop) and helicopter as ASW assets based on carriers. I wonder why there isn’t a capability for the NATO player to retask carriers for this purpose (maybe some prewar option?). I did some digging on the subject: carriers providing a platform for ASW assets to protect convoys and themselves. Evidently, the navy phased out the S3 in 2009, with an apparent lack of interest in using carriers in this manner given perceived current and future threats. I think this is a blind spot in current war planning. I found a few bits on the web that also seem to make this point: An article by Chris Woody, JAN 2019/Retreat from Range by Jerry Hendrix in 2015"They actually got rid of the S-3 early in the sense that the community still had a viable population of aircraft," Hendrix said. Their departure left a hole in carrier defenses that remains unfilled, especially when carrier groups are far from the airfields where P-8 Poseidons are based.More helicopters have been added to the carrier air wing, Hendrix said. "However, the helicopters don't have either the sensors or the mobility to be able to really patrol the middle zone" in which the S-3 operated. Nor does the arrival of the P-8 Poseidon — a vaunted maritime patrol aircraft introduced in 2013 to replace the P-3 — make up for the Viking's absence, according to Hendrix. "We haven't brought the P-8s in in a one-to-one replacement basis for the older P-3s, and so they're not really in sufficient numbers to do the middle-zone and outer-zone anti-submarine-warfare mission for the carrier strike groups," he said. "So we haven't filled that requirement in force structure." "ASW will become an increasingly important [carrier air wing] mission as adversary submarine forces increase in their size, sophistication, and ability to attack targets ashore and at sea using highly survivable long-range weapons," said a recent report on the carrier air wing by the Center for Strategic and Budgetary Assessments. A more aggressive China postureHefty RAND report: some interesting analysisMore aggressive China postureA number of reports on this item. RAND Charts from a few years ago below. Decent RAND report here: https://www.rand.org/content/dam/rand/pubs/research_briefs/R...  …and that will lead you to a hefty report on USA / CHINA capabilities. An interesting read….scroll to page 184…the Chinese Submarine Threat…” China’s submarine fleet is a centerpiece of its military modernization efforts and poses a significant and increasing threat to U.S. Navy surface assets operating in the region”. Interesting analysis contained in that RAND study.A future scenario? Hope not.A RAND assessment 6 years ago. Today?So, as with any good wargame, it has sparked interest in a subject I hadn’t thought much about…which will mean a trip to Amazon and the web to appease the curiosity bug. Can’t wait to add a ASW themed carrier group optional house rule and counter next time for giggles. Anyways, it appears the only reason to forwardly deploy carriers in the game is deliver bombs on soviet troops and engage the limited soviet surface fleet off of Norway – providing one could get there in time to make a difference. Back to the action…Attack on TF Hammer...So another wounded SOVIET sub attacked TF Hammer. Evading the ASW screen, the sub launched its torpedoes. Suddenly, an explosion on a USA carrier: the America was burning. SOVIETs gained their first NATO loss point (get 6, earn a Hammer & Sickle – SOVIETs need 4 H&S pts to win. The other Hammer & Sickles are earned by advancing troops on the various game tracks). USA was able to track down and sink the assassin, but, the damage was done. Premier JR smiled. T3D5N9: Another Orion was dispatched to find the wounder boomer and escort in W4-5. Again, the sneaky bastards avoided the clutches of the capitalist. TFs then moved. Soviets were able to sink a brave Norwegian subs: only one remained.Day 5 ended with a NATO Sturgeon continuing to hunt the pesky RED boomer and escort in the Caribbean. Again, no luck when its ASW proved ineffective.Probably a slight edge for the day to the evil empire. It had damaged a USA carrier and had laid the detection ground work of NATO TFs to reap the rewards on Day 6. However, it had suffered another slide towards Internal Coup: never a good thing.TURN 3: DAY 6: SOVIET Stability Goes WobblyDay begins with both places tossing a 12 Ops card into the mix.T3D6S1: Another ROSAT launched.T3D6N1; NATO tosses a LA class sub on patrol to E4T3D6S2: An attempt at upgrading detection of a TF sadly fails: someone will be held accountable.T3D6N2: More NATO boomer hunting E9-10. Two subs hit…including a boomer than is sunk. Total boomer payload loses now hit 16. One more boomer hit will trigger another Soviet Stability roll.T3D6S3: SOVIET successfully upgrade detection on another NATO TF; in this case, TF Viking.T3D6N3: NATO dispatches yet another Orion to patrol in E4.T3D6S4 hits on NATO TFsT3D6S4: SOVIET attempts to launch a sub attack on a TF in E4. NATO ASW successfully counters.T3D6N4: NATO again pursues the pesky boomer in the Caribbean. Dice gods smile on the REDS and grant a 3rd evasion to its sub.T3D6S5: Soviet Victor goes hunting for a TF in E4. Victor applies two hits, while NATO ASW negates one. None-the-less, the SOVIET hit punishes a UK carrier.T3D6N5 Boomer sunk 2 rollsT3D6N5: Yet another Orion attempts to hunt down the pesky boomer and escort in the Caribbean. This time, NATO finds success and both soviet interlopers dispatched to the bottom. Given the additional boomer playload loss, another SOVIET  STABILITY TRACK roll is triggered  - in fact two. When the smoke cleared, not only had the Politburo decided to intervene but RED Backfires were no prohibited from most strikes. The Soviet Union is now only two spaces away from an Internal Coup.T3D6N5B SOVIET STABILITY FAIL AGAINT3D6S6: Another Victor sub attacks a NATO Tf in E4. Again, success. This time, three hits are put on a NATO convoy.T3D6N6: Orion goes on patrol in E4T3D6S7: Another ROSAT is able to upgrade detection on TF Aegis to goodT3D6N7: NATO detects a secret nuclear storage facility in Sevastopol (a card play).T3D6N7 CARD SETS UP SEVASTAPOLT3D6S8: Persistent SOVIET sub attacks. NATO TF Aegis takes more punishment with additional hits.T3D6SHIP Three NATO TFs enters brest.....and the red light district in Brest encounters an economic boom.TF Ship move triggered. NATO subs head for the shelter of Brest. Hot time in that port. SOVIETs managed to kill the last Norwegian sub.TURN 3; DAY 6: late: Sin in Sevastopol: a Secret SOVIET Nuclear Storage Facility Discovered…and a STRIKE! T3D6S9: A Delta Victor sub targets a NATO TF in M8-9. However, no success.T3D6N9: A Thresher sub finds a SOVIET sub in N8-9. Another RED sub damaged. And another slide in SOVIET STABILITY. REDs were now 1 away from game ending.T3D6S10: Soviets send up another ROSAT. Next pulse would produce some drama.A moment of dramaT3D6N10: NATO decides to act on the intel that had revealed SOVIET skullduggery in Sevastopol: they had hid a nuclear stockpile in the Crimea. A strike package was prepared on the Kennedy and Kitty Hawk…and dispatched. We then discovered on the map “overflight Turkey: 1 zone”. It appeared that given that the Kennedy/Kitty Hawk were based in MED 5-6, they would not have the range to conduct the strike. JR, the consummate gentleman wargamer, commented, “You could have easily moved the TF from M5-6 to M7-8 in the Ship Phase we just had. Do that and let’s roll some dice and proceed with the drama”. The mission continued…The F14 escorts ran into CAP including Foxbats, Fishbeds and Floggers. A dogfight ensued. Soviets whiffed, but F14s found their mark: Foxbats destroyed and Fishbeds damaged. Next came the SAMs. NATO successfully suppressed some of the SAM. However, after the SAM scrum cleared, NATO was left with only one load of bombs. Two hits would be required to take out the secret SOVIET nuclear storage; meaning a 9 or 10 on a ten-sider. The NATO said a prayer. One lonely dice was tossed high into the air. It spun. Stopped. And out pop’d a magic “9”. Implication? Soviets would have to toss two dice on the SOVIET STABILITY Track. Dice tossed. An internal coup. A SOVIET cry of anguish. Game over. Evil empire defeated. The world would breathe easier on May 1.T3D6 N10 END OF THE LINEEnd of GameWrap upPlayMusic from 1983 for the Political Bureau of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union Our verdict on the game has not changed from our initial play: big thumbs up. The game produces a real tension between NATO desperately trying to get men and supplies to European war fronts and the SOVIETs taking risks attempting to grab First Strike Points (or getting them via cards), while not losing political stability. The trade-offs each player make are beefy – all within the context of many levers, knob and dials that can be pulled, pushed and spun to produce the thrill of victory or the agony of defeat.And, oh does it need a combination of better rules organization and/or a decent index. Oye. We spent a BUNDLE of time searching for this or that rule. Playaids need to be also indexed to the rules. The actual rules we thought are decent. We found no significant missing bits or internally non consistent logic or contradictory non sense. None. The only issue is that we found it VERY difficult to find answers to our questions. Eventually, we usually did. When we didn’t, we posted and the designer or a friend of the game would answer QUICKLY. Without that level of support, we likely would have tossed in the towel – despite this being an outstanding game that produces a fabulous storyline. We had so much fun we are planning to begin a rematch this week. Link to other 1st MN/Sawatdee/Herr Dr AARs:

tier2.author: djberg96
tier2.body: Coincidentally I've been going through the rules for PQ-17 by GMT games. In some ways it reminds me of BWN, basically focused on the same geographic area with a similar theme, only 45 years or so earlier using WW2 technology.One interesting concept that game has is shadowing, i.e. if a unit (air, sub or surface) detects an enemy task force, it can "shadow" the enemy task force in question instead of attack. The game effect is that it potentially improves future attacks against that task force, as well as retaining detection on it, preventing the normal automatic reduction each turn.The downside of shadowing is that you can't intercept/attack/detect other task forces that might move through their hex. In addition, you must move with that TF when it moves (it loses its own movement). Plus, you could lose your shadowing due to bad weather, the enemy fleet moving outside of air range or other reasons.Is this something that would make sense in 1980's warfare? Too much fiddle faddle? Or is the assumption that the shadowing is already abstracted into the rules as written?

tier2.body: I fear my strategy is predicated upon a fatal misreading of First Strike Points.  I thought I picked up one FSP for every six points of boomers I had in launch areas, but it looks like I get a maximum of one FSP if I have at least six points of boomers in launch areas. tier2.author: Herr
tier2.body: Background During COVID exile, one thing I binged was Occupied: a hybrid/little green men Russian operation in Norway. Good series.Related, I'm a big fan of Cold War goes hot games. It has been awhile since one struck my fancy. Found one: Blue Water Navy: The War at Sea {"BWN"}Fun game. Lots of depth to it. Meaty. This session report follows upon one from a few weeks ago: JR's Sea of Soviet Sorrows: 1983 Cold War Goes Hot: Blue Water Navy Spring 2021That session report covered turn 1 of the 1983 campaign game. This session report covers turn 2. Before that, a bit about the gameGame DynamicsI briefly examined the components of thee game in the first session report; a few additional thoughts...Soviet Stability Track One way NATO can win is to push the Soviet Union to internal coup: essentially a breaking of their strategic will. Strategic operational wargames should have a strategic will component. A few beloved masterpieces  have avoided it (ex:   ), but many contain it.  Here's how BWN works:1) Loss of soviet boomer subs (ICBMs) triggers a roll on a table2) Depending upon that roll, the Soviet Stability track may shift to the right (towards coup). Bad stuff happens as the track shifts to the right.A few comments:1) I wish other game items/player performance would have impacted it. The king of the hill of strategic will models remains   and   (which is actually Political "stability" Points - but, same dif). With both those fantastic wargames, MUCH impacts the strategic will track.2) I wish there was a NATO stability track. Why the omission? Good question. First Strike Points OPs points, pulse movement & TF movement Game does a great job of trying to simulate individual ship/planes (ship/airplane counters of course represent more than 1 ship/1 plane for the most part) mixed in with task forces. As with any pulse movement game tied to OPs points, a player is trying to arbitrage ops points: spend a few and cause your opponent to spend A LOT more reacting...and leave themself vulnerable somewhere. Deciding when in the turn to go provocative - or invest in setting up a bold move later - or improving your defense - is a BIG part of the puzzle. Just like our first session, we were both constantly running through pulse "angst" - and enjoying it.Combat resolution A ton of tables to cover a ton of different situations. At first, it appears daunting - and you'll go through a fair amount of frustration trying to find this or that applicable sequence (one rules misfire - the playaid sheets lack rules reference numbers...that covers to aggravate us).Having said that, we've found the combat resolution mechanics very engaging: good fun and great story line produced.Abstraction of land operationsI generally hate abstraction in wargames. Of course, all of the game is an abstraction, but I mean "roll on this table, you win Spain". BWN does a great job of providing all the levers and dials for air/sea, but using tracks to reflect the the air/sea outcome on the land war. Norway, Western Europe and Southern each get a track. NATO can attempt to slow Soviet progress on each front by bombing the hell out of each region.All-in-all, nothing in the mechanics bothers us. A very deep and rich game that produces great storyline.On to the session report.TURN 2: DAY 1: Thrust and Parry. RED Invade Norway I drew my cards to begin the second day. Soviets tossed a card and began the Day 3 (which is the first part of turn 2...each turn has 2 days).The day involved quite a bit of the Soviet Arctic Wolfpack making the run to East9-10. NATO AWS was ineffective (with one exception), added to its picket line and pushed its task forces forward.First impulse involved an LA class sub hitting else with the play of a dastardly soviet card: friendly fire. NATO launched a strike from the UK on the Soviet Task force off the cost of Norway - an attempt to disrupt the invasion. 6 missiles were launched...and, sadly, 6 missiles shot down.Day ended with NATO successfully hunting the two remaining subs off its Atlantic coast in West 2-3, by damaging both. However, another sneaky Soviet card negated one of the hits.Lowlight for NATO was Soviet troops finally pushing ashore in Norway: that would demand a response...and one was forthcoming TURN 2: DAY 2: NATO Thrashes Advancing Soviet Columns Red Hot Chili Peppers - By The Way [Official Music Video]PlayThere is a light on and a heavy glow in Southern Europe...commie tanks a  burnin'Kitty Hawk and Kennedy strike force sauté soviets in Southern Europe for another turnSoviets opened with running another sub through the Arctic to East 9-10 via North 9-10 underwater highway. A brave, but battered, LA class NATO defender scored a hit. Rejoice! Diabolical soviet player then whipped out a damm "double hull" card to negate the success.NATO then ordered a strike on Southern Europe from K&K (Kennedy & Kitty Hawk). When the smoke cleared, 3 more hits were scored on the impotent Soviet columns...meaning no advance, again, on that front. We then discussed how the Soviet player can defend against these strikes....we need to do further research to find an effective defense. Soviets continued building its HUGE Wolfpack in East 9-10. Another sub ran the gambit successfully.NATO then ordered a strike on Norway. During the Task Force movement impulse in the previous day, NATO had boldly (or recklessly) pushed carriers into North 5-6. Now, they struck. Flyboys from the America and the Enterprise left their flattops and proceeded east. Soviet SAM completely whiffed. Bombs away....SIX HITS; meaning the soviets would be stymied for two days. Norway avenged! This will teach JR to mess with Norway.Continuing the Arctic to East 9-10 run, another Soviet sub made the attempt. Again, the wounded, but brave, LA class found its mark. However, this time the Soviet sub made a save roll. However, when the accompanying soviet boomer tried to enter East 9-10, it was promptly found and sunk. This would have ramifications for Soviet Stability... [note: losing soviet boomers triggers a slide towards various nasty things for the commies].Soviet Premier watches as his deathstar Wolfpack grows in East 9-10Turn winded down with Soviets pushing another sub into East 9-10 and NATO strengthening its sub picket line in the North Atlantic...preparing for the upcoming Soviet blitz out of East 9-10. Final play of the turn was another sneaky Russian trick...in the form of trawler with a deck full of distracting soviet beauties in scanty swimsuits. As it inched closer to the NATO task force Aegis, all of a sudden a soviet sub appeared. The trawler turnout to be black widow. Task Force Aegis had been detected and branded for the attack. Luckily, a miss. End of Turn Wrap UpVictor's Song   Local HeroPlayFantastic movie...Local Hero...with Victor, the Russian trawler operator that almost brought ruin to a NATO task force, belting out a tune.We took a look at the War tracks: So Europe stuffed...Norway stuffed for two days...however, Soviets kept advancing in Central Europe. That could be real issue for NATO, given Hanover had now gone RED. We did the Soviet Stability table, now that Commie Man had two sunk boomers. Soviet Union slipped to Allies Waiver.The War Continues and We Are Having FunWe're continuing to have a great time and will resume, hopefully, this week with Turn 3. Our earlier assessment holds:1) MEATY wargame game...2) ...with a lot of dials and levers...3) ...healthy amount of "pulse angst" (what the hell do I do on this pulse, given all the threats and opportunities)4) ...full of flavor (decent chrome)5) ...innovative mix of game subsystems6) ...producing a great storyline.We'll see if the NATO ring of steel around the Soviet's East 9-10 Wolfpack holds on turn 3...if Soviet stability deteriorates...if Russia and friends continue their progress in Central Europe. At least the Norwegians will hold their own for a bit. Long live Norway...free of a Soviet yoke!Link to other 1st MN/Sawatdee/Herr Dr AARs:

tier2.author: LeSpass
tier2.body: Quote:A submarine may move and go On Patrol in one sea zone per turn.	CorrectQuote:A MP may move and go ‘On Patrol’ in up to three sea zones per turn, if it does not perform an attack.	If it is not spent, it can return to base and back ‘On patrol’ when you are active without becoming spent. The number of times a fresh MP unit can go 'On Patrol' is limited by the number of operation points.        For example. When active, you spend an operation point to put a MP unit 'On Patrol'. Now the other player goes active. When you are active again, you can return the MP back to base. It is not spent and does not consume the action. You can spend an operation point to put it back 'On Patrol'. Now the other player goes active. If the MP 'On Patrol' is triggered, it immediately goes back to base and becomes spent.Quote:If an MP does perform an attack while On Patrol, it is marked Spent.	CorrectQuote:An MP marked Spent may only be refreshed during End of Turn Phase, meaning it can only ambush one unit per turn (although it could potentially patrol (and influence) 3 different sea zones per turn if it makes no attack).	Indeed, it is spent once it is triggered. But as mentioned before, it can RTB multiple time. It is limited by the number of actions you have.Quote:A fighter may move and go On Patrol in three sea zones per turn, if it wants to.	Same thing as MP. If it is not spent, it can return to base and back ‘On patrol’ when you are active without becoming spent. The number of times a fresh fighter can go 'On Patrol' is limited by the number of operation points. To clarify, a non MP become ‘Fresh’ during the ‘Ships’ event and on the end of turn phase. A MP only at the end of turn phase. (9.1.3. Point six of 'Ships' event)Quote:A fighter is also not considered Spent when it performs an attack while On Patrol so it can perform multiple intercepts per turn.	Correct

tier2.author: BravoCo
tier2.body: Hi,I want to make sure I understand the nuances here:A submarine may move and go On Patrol in one sea zone per turn.  This is because On Patrol cannot be removed until End of Turn Phase.  If a submarine performs an attack while On Patrol, it is marked Spent, meaning it can only ambush one unit per turn (notwithstanding nuances in 6.8).A MP may move and go On Patrol in up to three sea zones per turn, if it does not perform an attack.This is because an On Patrol MP can be returned to base every time it is the player's turn to play an action, but it is not considered an action. If an MP does perform an attack while On Patrol, it is marked Spent.An MP marked Spent may only be refreshed during End of Turn Phase, meaning it can only ambush one unit per turn (although it could potentially patrol (and influence) 3 different sea zones per turn if it makes no attack).A fighter may move and go On Patrol in three sea zones per turn, if it wants to.This is because an On Patrol fighter can be returned to base every time it is the player's turn to play an action.  Note: maybe 16.6.4 should only apply during a ship move so it comports with 16.3, paragraph 5.A fighter is also not considered Spent when it performs an attack while On Patrol so it can perform multiple intercepts per turn.Did I get all of the above correct?

tier2.author: LeSpass
tier2.body: If ten missiles went through the SAM, you get three nukes and seven regular missiles. Resolve nukes first. Nukes always hit and kill the target except if it is a convoy/amphibious which causes three damage hits. The hits are allocated by the attacker on an 8+.  Roll one die for every nuke to decide who allocates the hits. (i.e. soviet rolls nuke allocation for three nukes with 5,7,9. Nato allocates the 5,7 and the soviet the 9)After the nuclear strike is finished, resolve the regular hits. With seven missiles, you get to roll three dice for the missile pairs and one die for the single remaining. Then allocate the hits as per 17.17 to whatever is remaining from the nuclear strike.

tier2.author: TFGA73
tier2.body: I’ve won with the Soviets twice, and one was actually rather easy (I think it ended on Turn 9). A few tips/observations:—Forget trying to take the Ruhr.   Do enough to keep NATO honest and spend resources protecting the Atlantic convoys, but the easiest route to four hammer and sickles is Oslo/Copenhagen/Milan/Rome.  With that said:—The Soviet army only has to advance in six turns to get to Rome.  NATO only gets five convoys to the Med.   Assuming you take Oslo and Copenhagen, taking out just one of the convoys at the right time can put NATO in a serious bind, especially if their carrier wings get worn down attacking Yugoslavia. — Use the random events, and if you pull Libya Active, keep it.  You can base bombers there and can attack all the way out past Gibraltar.    I’ve found that no other event alters the strategic calculus as much.   This makes US carriers vulnerable in the Med.  They cannot afford to send F14s in raids on Yugoslavia because of the increased bomber threat.  Thus the CAGs get worn down much faster. —Though it sounds counterintuitive the Russians actually do better in the 89 game when they have the better subs and a little more surface strength.  Their additional units seem to have more of an impact than NATO’s.—Think wolfpack with your subs and set up your at-sea units around the edges at the start.   In one game I piled 6 nuke subs in the Labrador Sea and had them lie in wait until the convoys came nearby.  Kilos and Tangos work great lying off Norfolk.  Convoys have to pass right over them and they’re tough to kill.   Pairing weak and strong subs is a good idea too.  The weaker one can sometimes get a lucky follow-up shot after the good sub does its bit.  —Don’t forget about the RORSATS.  A huge advantage if placed properly (Bay of Biscay, Western Med, etc). —Only use Backfires against a sure thing.   They are your trump card.  Hold them back until they can make a decisive strike.  —Forget sending boomers out for FSPs, unless it’s the Typhoon or Delta IV and you’re feeling feisty.  Not worth the risk.  Boomer losses are the Soviets Achilles heel and are NATO’s easiest route to a back-door victory.  —Always remember that the Soviets have the initiative.  They only have to focus on parts of the map to win.   NATO has to be everywhere.   Spread them out, wear them down, and it can be done.

tier2.body: From my point of view, is just a matter of relative capability. If you look at the other detection assets available to detect Task Forces, three or four submarines using sonar have a very limited detection chance on a 500nm wide area.Compare it for example to a maritime patrol unit that has 15 aircraft all equipped with long search radars and the area that they can cover. Then you have radar satellites which have 1 die.Active sonar has a very limited range and at long ranges, it relies on convergence zones on which the target has to be in order to be detected. Additionally, sonar performance depends heavily on weather and sea conditions (Thermal layer, ducts, etc...)For detecting ships, radar is just way too good compared to sonar.

tier2.body: Kirov’s and carriers AAROptional rules in effect:- Each player draws five cards which can be used for reaction events.- 30.3 Bombs Away!Only rolling for weather on east and north areas, as the other are not relevant for the scenario. Rolling 6 on East. This gives one die of bad weather. Rolling for sea zone allocation with a 10. East 9-10 has bad weather. Rolling 3 on North. Clear weather on North.Rolling for damage on Keflavik and the Scottish airbases as per the special rules. Roll 8 and 6 respectively. 2 hits on Keflavik and 1 on Scotland.Scenario setup.USSR divides their ship fleet into two Task Forces.- TF Gorshkov with the Kresta and Sov-Udaloy groups, an amphibious flotilla and some Victor I escorting subs.- TF Andropov with the Minsk and its air complement of Yaks (useless pieces of rust), the Kirov, Kynda group and Victor III escorting submarines.USSR Task Forces.NATO has its forces in two Task Forces as well.- TF Viking has the Enterprise with its air complement, the US-3 surface group, and an escorting Sturgeon.- TF Ranger has the Saratoga with its air complement, the US-1 & US-7 surface groups and some escorting Sturgeon boats.NATO Task Forces.USSR launches two regiment of Badgers against airbases in the UK. Two Phantoms roll for CAP (the maximum number of CAP fighters is limited by the size of the air strike). They roll one die less per squadron due to light damage in the airbase. Roll 6-8-2-8 + 1 Tactical. 2 hits that the attacker can save on a 6+ for attacking a land facility. Roll 3-9, one step loss on the Badgers.12 missile strike inbound. This turn into 2 dice for cruise missiles against land facilities. Roll 8-10. 3 hits plus 3 step losses of collateral damage. Odd losses allocated by the attacker. First step allocated to the Buccaneers, second to one of the Nimrods, and the third to the remaining Buccaneer step.This strike compromises the overall NATO capability to control the combat area and has its strike power completely wiped out. Badgers are spent. USSR 8 Ops remaining.The Scottish Airbases are going to be out of comission for a while.Fast Task Forces may now move. TF Andropov moves first into the Norwegian sea. TF Viking moves to East 6 while TF Ranger remains in place.Ships are getting closerNATO launches the Orion stationed in Norway to try detect TF Andropov. The Russian Yaks roll for disruption. They roll 9, disrupting the Orion, who has no dice to roll. Orion is spent. NATO 8 Ops remaining.Disrupted by Yaks, really?Op track repairs are performed. Iceland 1 hit, UK 3 hits.USSR time to detect the enemy Task Forces. They send the Bear D. Enterprise’s F-14 roll for disruption with 2 dice (4 minus 2 for disrupting MP). Roll 4-9 +2 Tactical, they disrupt the Bear. It still has one die left to roll for detection. Roll 6. Poor Detection placed by the rolling player. TF Viking is detected. After almost having a heart attack, the Bear crew return to base. Bear-D is spent. USSR 7 Ops remaining.Will the soviets be able to make a chink on the Task Force armor?USSR proceeds with a follow on attack with the Tango submarine on East 6. It roll with 2 dice (4 minus 2 for attacking a Fast TF with a Diesel boat). Rolls 2-7 for one hit PM hit.TF Viking has a ASW value of 12 (Bkd Sturgeon +6, US-3 +4, Enterprise +2). Being a Fast TF degrades its ASW capability to 3 dice to defend itself. Rolls 5-7-9. It stops the attack but the Tango goes slips away. This was not the result that the soviets expected.Tango is spent. USSR 6 Ops remaining.NATO, rattled by the sudden appearance of soviet boats, calls for help inland. The Atlantique on France flies to East 6 to patrol the area. NATO 7 Ops remaining.Ships may now move. TF Viking remains in place. TF Andropov goes to East 6 to meet the carriers. TF Ranger remain in place. TF Gorshkov moves to the Norwegian Sea. TF Viking is no longer detected.Things are about to get hot.Carrier fighters scramble for combat. Tomcat pilots are eager for some kills, but the Yaks seem a bit reluctant. Soviet command orders the Yaks to engage, but one pilot says that he can’t hear because the radio is broken, another one says that is short on fuel, another says that the plane is flying backwards, and so on. There will definitely be time in Siberia for those pilots back home if they manage to survive. Yaks refuse to engage in combat and they are spent.F-14 roll to disrupt the Minsk Kamov AEW helicopters with two dice. Rolls 1-9 (need 6+), disrupting the only die the Minsk has for detection. TF Viking sends a Hawkeye to detect TF Andropov with two dice. Rolls 10-10 placing a Good Detection on TF Andropov.Bad spot to be in for TF Andropov.Spent markers removed from non MP air units.Ships event is finished.Things are not looking good for the soviets. CAGs have been briefed and are ready to go. Enterprise and Saratoga striking assets fly to attack TF Andropov. They have little chance but the question is, will stall NATO enough for TF Gorshkov to land in Norway?Forgers roll for CAP with one die (Even though they are spent, the minimum dice number is one anyways). Roll 7 for no effect. The Intruders launch their Harpoons. 12 missile strikes inbound. TF Andropov launches all their SAMs. Defender needs to roll 3-8 to shoot down a missile strike and 9+ to shoot down two -1 DRM for defending against NATO missiles. Roll 3-4-4-1-2-7. 10-10-1-9. They manage to shoot 5 missile strikes. Seven missile strikes inbound. This gives 1 die for every pair of strikes and 1 for the single remaining. Rolls have +1 DRM for Good Detection on defending Task Force. Roll the single first with a 10, 2 hits. Roll the rest 1-7-10. 3 additional hits. NATO rolls for missile allocation. They need a 9 or 10 on a 2 dice roll. Roll 1-4. The defender will allocate the first hit. and NATO attacking will allocate every second one: Red-Blue-Red-Blue-Red. First to the Kynda group, Second to the Kirov, third to the Kynda. Fourth to the Minsk and the fifth to the Minsk.Kirov and Minsk roll for capital ship damage. The Kirov has one hit allocated, so it roll with 1 die (one for hits with NATO missiles). It will sink on an 8+. Rolls 8. The Kirov is lost.The Minsk roll two die for damage one for hits with NATO missiles another one for an additional hit received). Rolls 3-4, it manages to stay afloat. The air complement will take a step loss on a 6+. Rolls 8. The Yaks are destroyed (1 step unit). So much on the travel plans for those rebelling pilots.Wait what, still more strikes to come?Is not over yet… The Intruders may be finished, but the Corsairs are knocking at the door with the Walleyes. TF Andropov if it can still be called Task Force, doesn’t have any anti air defense against the incoming bombers. The CAGs have a total of 4 dice for bombing. Roll 6-8-5-6. Minsk receives 4 hits.Minsk roll for capital ship damage once again. 1 die for receiving NATO bombs (here I assumed that it has the same effect as a NATO missile strike), another one for being already damaged and one more for each additional hit taken at the same time for a whole total of 5 dice. Rolls 1-5-5-6-8. The Minsk is sunk.It was a massacre. TF Andropov is destroyed. The escorting Victor III will fight for retribution. NATO carrier CAGs are spent. NATO 3 Ops remaining.Only the Victor remains.USSR launches their Bear-F to spot the NATO Task Forces. Enterprise’s Tomcats try to disrupt it. Roll 2 dice. It will disrupt on a 9+ and cause a step loss on a N10. Rolls 1-2 for no effect. The Bear rolls one die for TF detection. Rolls 9, Good Detection allocated by the rolling player. TF Ranger is detected. Bear F is spent. USSR 5 Ops remaining.NATO's turn to get guttered?Victor III boats launch the follow on attack. They roll 4 dice (+1 against a Good Detection TF, -1 for attacking a Fast TF). Rolls 1-9-5-5 +1 Tactical which turn into 2-10-6-6. Victor III has heavy torpedoes, which turn the 10 into a N10, and both 6 hits, into hit to PM hits.TF Ranger has am ASW value of 21 (Sturgeon +9, US-7 +4, US-1 +3, Enterprise +2, Atlantique ‘On Patrol’ +3). Being a Fast TF deteriorates the ASW capability to 4 dice. Rolls 2-7-7-8. US-1 & US-7 groups are equipped with rocket torpedoes. This can change the double 7 into a single 8. In total, two attack dies are stopped and one PM hit allocated by the attacker punches the Task Force. US-1 group is flipped. Victor III is spent. USSR 4 Ops remaining.Barely a vengeance for the soviets. Tough luck.Ops track repairs are performed. 2 hit damage on the UK and Iceland is fully repaired.Suspecting an air strike on the TF Ranger, NATO transfers the US-3 group from TF Viking to TF Ranger. They have to be careful. TF Viking may not be detected, but they have no surface escorts, although the soviets do not know this fact yet. NATO 2 Ops remaining.Soviets do know though, that US-3 joined TF Ranger. The planned air strike has been canceled. No Maritime Patrol aircraft are available, and trying to detect TF Viking with submarines is basically useless. They decided to launch a RORSAT and hope for the best. The rocket launching the satellite will malfunction on a N1 with one die. Rolls 6. There is a RORSAT over East 6. USSR 2 Ops remaining.Ships may now move. TF Ranger stays in place. TF Gorshkov drop the landing marker. Rolls for detection with one die due to landing operations. Rolls 7. TF Gorshkov is poorly detected They will land on the next chance to move. TF Viking remains in place. Carrier Task Forces remain in place to be able to attack the landing forces in time. Moving through the GUIK Gap will be a suicide with all the submarine assets available for the soviets, and moving to other Sea Zones will leave them without the range for the aircraft to attack.Soviets don't lose any time. We need those men on shore ASAP.TF Ranger has its detection degraded to Poor. RORSAT rolls for detection. Rolls 5. Poor Detection placed by the TF owner unless upgrading. TF Ranger is upgraded to Good Detection. Spent markers removed from non MP air units.Ships event finished.NATO decides, they need to strike the landing forces immediately. They send both CAGs to attack TF Gorshkov.CAGs reach TF Gorshkov. The Intruders launch their Harpoons. 12 missile strikes inbound. Is so overkill, is not even funny. Soviets are desperate. They launch every single SAM they have. The defender needs to roll 3-8 to shoot down a missile strike and 9+ to shoot down two -1 DRM for defending against NATO missiles. Roll 5 dice for 9-10-1-3-8. They manage to shoot 4 missile strikes.Eight Harpoon strikes inbound. This gives 1 die for every pair of strikes for a total of 4. Roll 8-10-2-4 giving 6 hits. NATO rolls for missile allocation. They need a 9 or 10 on a 2 dice roll. Roll 8-9. The attacker will allocate the first hit and NATO attacking, every second one: Blue, Blue, Red, Blue, Red, Blue. First and second go to the amphibious flotilla. Third one to the Kresta group. Fourth to the amphibious flotilla again. Fifth to the remaining of the Kresta. Sixth to the Sov-Udaloy group. Every missile hit does 2 damage to an amphibious unit and is destroyed on 5 hits. With 6 damage hits, the amphibious flotilla is destroyed. A step of the Sov-Udaloy group is the only surface force left on the Task Force.Corsairs go to finish the job. The defender has one SAM die attack for every 3 SAM points of the Task Force. It only has 2 left, meaning that the bombing is completely unhampered. CAGs have 4 dice for bombing. Roll 5-5-7-10, all allocated by the attacker. Sov-Udaloy is sunk and TF Gorshkov is destroyed. The Victor I boats are the only survivors.Again, only the subs remain. Minute of silence for the fallen.CAGs are spent. NATO has no Ops remaining.NATO total victory.At the end, soviet plans for Norway will have to wait for another time.I used the Bombs away! optional rule to show more mechanics and increase the utility of the AAR. It didn’t make much difference, as the Missile attack already crippled the defenders.The game was tighter that the results would led to believe. Some different results on the detection rolls, and on NATO carrier would have been under attacks from TF Andropov then subsequent attacks from Kola, and the TF Gorshkov would have landed undetected or with better chances of survival.The USSR side really missed their tankers on this one. A Twelve missile strike would have really made the difference, but with six due to reduced payload for range, is just not possible to punch through.Thoughts?

tier2.author: fatgreta
tier2.body: Blue Water Navy AARKirovs and CarriersTurn 1The Soviets have a powerful surface Task Force in The Barents Sea ready to invade Trondheim. There are 2 US Carrier Groups on station south of the GIUK Gap, and they are the only opposition at the moment. Soviet missile attacks have damaged both Keflavik and Stornaway, grounding air units there. Soviet strike aircraft on the Kola Penninsula sit armed and ready. A horde of Soviet submarines patrol the waters. Can NATO protect Norway?Bad weather slowed the Soviet task force, but by the end of the turn it has begun unloading troops and not suffered any damage. NATO has repaired its bases, but even so has been ravaged. Multiple strikes by Russian Badgers and a swarm of submarines have devastated US Naval forces, eliminating an entire Task Force including the carrier. Most of the Russian strike aircraft have been destroyed. Even so, available NATO forces for striking at the Soviet amphibious units are now reduced by one full CAG. And the fighting has only just begun…Turn 2The Soviets opened the turn with a sub launched cruise missile attack against the Scottish airbases, since the US TF was not yet detected. They wanted to keep the UK strike aircraft grounded and caused light damage. NATO failed its repair roll, then had a choice to make. They moved their remaining Carrier into waters NE of Iceland to avoid satelite detection, then sent an MP to improve the poor detection on the Soviet amphibious TF, which they would have followed up with an air strike (albeit a weak one). The Soviet Yak-38’s did their job though, turning the patrol back before it could mount a search. This was devastating to NATO, as the next Soviet ops triggered the Ships event, which led to a resolution of the Amphibious Landing. A lone Norwegian sub sortied and tried to stop the enemy, but failed. And that is when some of what is great about this game showed up.To summarize, when landing troops the Soviets roll dice to see what kind of resistance the landing is being met by. Then, depending on the capabilities of the TF conducting the landing, they may or may not fight through that resistance. In game play terms dice are rolled, numbers on units are consulted and math is done to see if the landing takes place, and how many troops get ashore. The Soviets got their full complement of two troops ashore and won the game. That is kind of dull though. As you go through the procedures to conduct the landing, a narrative is created about what NATO is doing on defense, and what the Soviets are countering with. Here is the narrative for the end of this particular game:The Norwegian General looked out across the water at Soviet amphibious landing vehicles making their way ashore. “If those troops land, we are doomed,” he realized. A water spout emerged from beneath a Soviet ship. Scanning with binocular, hoping to see a troop ship sinking, the General instead noted that a Soviet Udaloy class destroyer was smoking and listing to port. Not sinking, though, and the ship was still firing munitions at the sub which had just wounded it. ‘That may help our allies,” he thought, “as the war progesses, but it will not help me hold this base.”As he thought that he took note of a flotilla of fast attack craft sortied, hoping to close the range and be able to fire their Penguin SSMs. As he watched, a horde of Soviet missiles appeared in the sky. Morosely, he observed those missiles strike home, and as the smoke cleared he saw only a few sailors trying to stay afloat. The only ship still afloat looked like it would not be for much longer.“Fire all missiles,” the General ordered, “they’re our last hope.” Surface based SSM’s streaked from launchers on shore, but many, many more SAM’s flew off the rails of the Soviet fleet. The last hope of stopping the Soviets from landing a large amphibious contingent was dashed.“Send this over all radio nets: ‘All commands, Masada. I say again, Masada.’” Masada was the code word for the order to hold in place at all costs. Picking up his rifle as he loaded into his command vehicle, the General ordered “Get us to the front lines, right now! We will hold them off as long as we are able.”

tier2.author: LeSpass
tier2.body: Air strike units can save CAP hits by meeting these conditions (rule 17.7, Detection Status and Air Strike Saves Table):- Hits from CAP of an airfield or a Good Detection Task Force can be avoided on a 6+.- Hits from CAP of a Poor Detection Task Force which is not the target of the air strike can be avoided on an 8+.Hits from CAP of a Poor Detection Task Force which is the target of the airstrike cannot be saved by  the above mentioned rule. Neither the hits of CAP from an undetected Task Force.Still, if the Soviet player has the ECM technology, Backfire and Bear-G have an 8+ save on all CAP and interceptions (rule 25.0). This is ignored if they already have a better save (Not in addition).
