tier2.author: acb3
tier2.body: This is my 3rd play thru of Scenario 1/1a. I wanted to do an AAR to force me to think thru/explain the rules as well as start to wrestle with strategy. Feel free to comment on either point.The US Player must sink Soviet SSBN's to win. VP points are based on SSBN Payload points damaged/sunk. The Soviet Player can reduce this by getting submarines across the SOSUS Barrier to attack incoming Convoys (not represented in the Scenario just assumed). The US player can also get a Payload VP by damaging/sinking the Kiev or pushing Soviet Yankees away from the First Strike areas. In scenario 1 the only Soviet SSBN's are in the Soviet Boomer Bastion north of the Barents. Scenario 1a adds a pair of Yankee SSBNs (and their escorts) in First Strike positions near the US East coast as added targets. Scenario lasts 3 turns.First decision is where to setup the Yankees in the First Strike zones:Far away from US SSN's to prevent first turn attack and all concentrated in one zone so when the attack occurs, both Yankee escort SSNs can counterattackNext roll for weatherWest - 2 ClearMid - 6 ClearNorth - 7 roll 2 die - zones N-1 (North Sea) and N-4 (Baltic)Maybe leverage the North Sea as a destination since weather makes it harder to detect/attack submarines?Each side gets 7 Ops points each turn (small scenario ops rules - no card play)Soviet's first ops - previous plays I had the November in N7-8 East of Iceland try to run the SOSUS array and force the UK SSN Swiftsure to attempt to kill. It would become spent in the process thus opening the way for the Alfa to make its run unopposed except for the patrolling P-3 on the other side.But the scenario is primarily about protecting the Soviet Boomers in the Bastion so the Soviets need to get as many ASW assets into the Bastion as soon as possible. Since 7 Ops on the track is a SHIP op also, instead I spend 2 Ops to form a Task Force with the Northern Fleet units in Kola Naval Base and sortie into the Barents Sea in preparation for moving into the Bastion later in the turn. One of the Victors already in the Bastion will join when it enters to increase its ASW effectiveness.For the US Op the LA SSN in the Norwegian Sea is going to try to preemptively damage or sink the Alfa so that when it does try to run the SOSUS barrier there is less chance it will make it. There is another LA on the other side of the SOSUS between Iceland and Scotland, the UK Swiftsure and a P-3 via the Northern SOSUS route. But if the Alfa goes to the North Sea then only a Nimrod and Bad Weather. Better do something now to prevent it from getting the VPs for crossing SOSOS.The LA gets 3 dice and +1 Tactical DRM, but the Alfa can evade hits on a 6+.Unbelievable - 10, 10, 10 on the VASSAL roller - never saw that before.Now 3d10 to see how many evaded - 4, 6, 10 - the Alfa was dancing and evaded 2 - but still damaged now.The LA is now Spent.Back to the Soviets. The Alfa is in a use it or lose it situation. If she does not try to run the SOSUS barrier now there is a good chance the US will do a follow on attack to try to finish her off. 3 choices per above - the 2 Iceland routes each have an SSN waiting - while the North Sea only has a Nimrod and Bad Weather or… the Danish Diesel boat in the Norwegian Sea. When crossing a SOSUS barrier a Soviet sub can be attacked by fresh US units from either side. As long as I am interpreting the scenario VP rules correctly (cross any SOSUS barrier) the obvious route is the North Sea because the Kobben has no tactical advantage DRM and the Nimrod is hampered by bad weather as well as requiring natural 10's to hit. So the Alfa runs for the North Sea and the Kobben takes her best shot…Kobben gets 3 dice +1 Dice for SOSUS detection - 1, 2, 5, 7 - all less than the Alfa's 9 Defense so a total miss. A slow Diesel boat versus a hot rod Alfa off to the races. The Alfa makes it across the SOSUS barrier and this gives the Soviet -1 Payload point VP against the US total. Per the scenario instructions, the Alfa is removed from the board. Correct me if I am wrong with my Scenario rules interpretations.Now back to the US. At this point the November instead of crossing the SOSUS barrier around Iceland can instead make a run South thru the Norwegian Sea (where both allied subs are spent) and then into the North Sea with only a Nimrod in bad weather able to stop her. The US player needs to attack the November now - but which sub should do it? The Swiftsure is able to move thru the Barents and into the Bastion and perform an attack this turn BEFORE the Northern Fleet ASW task force can take station. The 2nd LA could do a high speed (3 moves) run into the Bastion but no attack. So the LA is better used moving and attacking the November, and the Swiftsure is still Fresh to either stop the November if it survives and if not make a run into the Bastion.The LA gets 3 dice and a +1 DRM - 3, 4, 7 - so 1 hit (7+1=8) and the November does not get evasion. And now I just realized a big oops. Since the LA attacked no one is guarding the SOSUS barrier between Iceland and Scotland. And that is where the November goes to get 1 more negative VP…Contrasting LA skippers - one attacks a high-speed Alpha and nails it with 10, 10, 10 - even an Alfa can't run from that kind of shooting. The other LA skipper leaves his position thinking he can take the November but then can't close the deal and the November slips out, albeit damaged.After the US expends 2 more ops points another move TF/SHIP event occurs, and the Soviet ASW TF will enter the Bastion. The defense of the SOSUS barrier phase is over, so its time to get all available SSNs into the Bastion. First to go is the Swiftsure via the Barents Sea. And the Victor III reacts upon its entry with an attack.She gets 3 dice +1 dice for the Soviet CAESAR Barrier (Soviet version of SOSUS) and a +1 DRM.But the Swiftsure can evade…The Victor rolls 2, 3, 5, 10 - 1 hit. The Swiftsure rolls evasion - 5!The Swiftsure is damaged but can still carry out her attack.She gets 2 dice and a +1 DRM - 6, 9 which translates to 7, 10 with +1 DRM.The weakest subs in the Bastion are the Delta I/II with defense of 8, but the 7 die roll is not enough so no effect for that roll.The 10 die roll can damage any sub in the Bastion, even the mighty Typhoon (but it can evade unlike the Deltas).But the DEFENDER gets to pick the target for the FIRST hit - which means one of the SSN's has to eat the hit to protect the Boomers. Even though the Victor III is better than the Victor II - it is spent and more subs are coming so the Victor II needs to stay ready.The Soviet now decides to start beefing up the Bastion with Maritime Patrol acft to add to the ASW TF when it arrives. The IL38 May with a range of 2 moves into the Bastion and goes on patrol. The Bears with a range of 3 are being saved for possible attacks on US subs outside of the Bastion.After the US expends its next op the Soviet ASW TF can move into the Bastion. Therefore the Sturgeon lurking under the ice in the Arctic starts its run into the Bastion now before that happens. Since the Sturgeon's defense is 10 (but it can not evade) and the Victor II does not have a +1 DRM, the MP limitation of Natural 10's to hit a nuclear submarine is not a negative in this situation. And the newly patrolling IL38 will get 3 +1 dice while the Victor II will get 2 +1 dice for CAESAR. So the IL38 prosecutes the Sturgeon.3 ASW Dice +1 dice for the CAESAR barrier and needs a natural 10 to hit. She rolls 1, 3, 9, 9 - whiff!The Sturgeon now gets an unopposed attack - unless she rolls a 1 and Bastion intrinsic defense damages her.She rolls 3 dice with a +1 DRM - 5, 9, 10 - effectively x2 10's and the Attacker gets to pick the 2nd hit.The Soviet wants to keep the Victor I intact to combine with the ASW TF when it arrives, so the Victor II eats another hit and is gone. The US could apply the 2nd hit to the Typhoon but it gets an opportunity to evade on 6+. Not wanting to take that chance, the US picks a Delta III to damage which gives 3 payload VPs. And at the end of the US op it is time to move TF's - so the Northern Fleet TF Borodino enters the Bastion ready to work with the remaining Victor II for coordinated ASW ops…The Soviet has 2 ops left and there are no more US subs that can get into the Bastion this turn. So it is time to setup to try to slowdown the remaining 2 US LA SSN's that can try to attack the Bastion next turn. The first op is spent sortieing the Foxtrot in Kola Naval Base into the Barents sea and going on patrol. This is the only path the US SSNs can use next turn to enter the Bastion and be able to attack also. The Arctic/Under Ice route will take 2 turns, and time is of the essence…Now that the major events in the North are almost done, the US shifts focus to the Western Atlantic and Caribbean where a number of Yankees are lurking. They could be critical to the US achieving its Payload VP condition since each SSBN has 4 payload points. If things don't go well in the Bastion this is where the US could pickup the missing points for victory. The Yankees are currently off the coast of Central America and out of range of the US SSNs off the coast of Nova Scotia for an attack this turn. So they need to get in position for attacks next turn. First, the LA moves to the First Strike area near Haiti/Puerto Rico. From this position even if the Yankees make a 3 space speed run next turn they are still within 2 space range of the LA and an attack. Not putting the LA On Patrol since that would freeze it in place and then it is easily avoided. The Sturgeon will also join the LA and the Roosevelt Roads P-3 will go on Patrol with the last ops.But first the Soviet expends its last op by sending a Bear from Kola to take a shot at the damaged Swiftsure and prevent it from attacking next turn. The Bear gets 3 ASW dice and needs a natural 10 for a hit… and the Swiftsure can evade. Long shot but worth the shot… 2, 6, and 10! Swiftsure rolls for evasion… 9! And she lives another day. The Bear returns to base.Maybe I should have put the Bear on patrol instead of rolling the dice?And in the Western Atlantic the US expends its remaining Ops points and sets up for next turn's Yankee hunt.I posted this AAR for 2 reasons:1. Get familiar with the rules. This is my 3rd play thru and I am finally feeling more comfortable that I am not making mistakes. But feel free to chime in if there are any.2. Start thinking thru strategy. Too many things to do and not enough ops points… Feel free to chime in on this also.Turn 2 soon - the Bastion will heat up and the hunt will be on in the Eastern Atlantic/Caribbean.

tier2.body: Hello folks,Since the release of BWN, I've been intensively studying the fleets of the WarPact and NATO, and I noticed one thing that provides the basis for a discussion in my opinion. Maybe there are some people who are interested in this topic as well and would like to give their opinion, that's why I am starting this thread.It's about the values of the surface ships. I analyzed the composition of all ship groups and took a closer look at the weapon loadout of all ships on the basis of various sources. And I noticed that some of the values are either lower than they could theoretically be or sometimes higher than historical plausible. To give an example, let's take the Krivak ASW Groups. The values in BWN are 2 SAM Points and 3 White Missile Points. According to the surface unit Reference on page 42 in the rulebook, those 2 groups each consist of 6 Krivak Is, 2 Krivak IIs and 2 Mod. Kildins. If I understand the rules correct, 1 Missile Point in BWN equals 8 Missiles in the real world. So, according to BWN those ships had around 24 SSMs available. However, according to one of my sources the only ships in this group that carried Anti-Ship Missiles were the Kildins, with 4 Missiles each. So, in my opinion the group should only have 1 White Missile Point, to account for the 8 SS-N-2c Styx missiles carried by the Kildins.On the other hand, the SAM value of this group seems lower than I would expect it to be, considering 1 SAM in BWN equals 16 Missiles and all the ships together in the real world would have carried way over 200 SAM Missiles.So, here is a certain discrepancy between the values used and the values I have calculated based on different sources. How do you guys feel about this topic?By the way, this is not supposed to be a criticism of the game, but I am simply interested in this topic and would like to know on which basis the values in the game were calculated and how realistic they are.

tier2.body: Stu, let me see if I can net out the question:In the main rules and using regular Ops track, based on on card-provided Ops points, both sides will always start above the "trigger points" for Ops track events. So events simply trigger as soon as the action is completed that results in both sides being at or below the relevant point the track.In the small scenarios, the turn can start with each side at or below the trigger point based on pre-determined Ops points. Scenario special rule #2 covers what to do for the events above both sides' markers - the events are resolved at the start of the turn. But it doesn't cover what to do if the highest marker is on the trigger point at turn start. Example: in scenario 1, at turn start the Soviet marker is on the SHIPS event (7 Ops), while NATO is below it (5 Ops). You clarified above that in this case, the Soviets are allowed to move their TF immediately at turn start: "Yes the Soviet TF can move right away as the event triggers right after the Soviet ops." This implies that for smaller scenarios where the highest Ops marker is on the event trigger point at turn start, that event is resolved after the initial action. I think Terry is trying to confirm that implication.To continue the example...Turn 1 - the Soviets spend 2 Ops to form the TF in port (7 > 5 Ops) and then immediately move it to sea due to SHIPS event (Ops 7). When SHIPS event (Ops 3) triggers, the TF can move again. At the start of turn 2, the Soviet Ops are reset to 7. This is below the FAST event, so the TF (which only has combatants and is fast) can immediately move again. As soon as the Soviets do their first action, the ships EVENT (Ops 7) triggers and the TF can move again, and again in SHIPS event (Ops 3). In other words, if the Soviets form the TF as their initial action of the scenario, then by the end of the second turn it could potentially move 5 times (2 in first turn, 3 in second turn).Is that correct? It's a very fun scenario and this impacts the TF's ability to interact with the NATO subs significantly.

tier2.author: daveb1971
tier2.body: This is kind of a mixed post.  Part Action update, part rules check.  If this is inappropriate please let me know.  These are some of the opening moves of a practice campaign game.  If anyone sees anything amiss I welcome the feedback.Operations PhaseSoviet Card - Strike US Targets 12pts NATO Card - Fast ConvoySoviet First ActionThe Soviet player pays two operations points to activate an Oscar-1 SSGN (East-3) and an Oscar-2 SSGN (East-2) and move to attack a detected TF Black (Poor) in MID-3 using missile coordination.  The Soviet player also plays the reaction card "Missile Coordination".  The Soviet player rolls to determine the Missile attack type with no modifier; normally this would have been -2 per additional submarine but reaction card negates this effect.  The Soviet player rolls 1D10.  The Soviet player rolls 8 resulting in a short-range attack.  Six yellow missiles are launched at TF Black.  TF Black contains the CV-Dedalo, Spanish surface units, Convoy-Med unit, and the Sea Harriers embarked on the carrier.  SAM point value for the TF is 2 (Spanish surface only).  NATO player rolls 2D10.  NATO rolls 7 and 8, which are modified by -2 (Yellow missile, no modifier for short-range because it is yellow) so modified 5 and 6.  Two missiles eliminated, four remain.  As there are four missiles, they roll 2D10 on the Incoming Missile Resolution chart under 2 missiles column.  Soviets roll a 2 and 5 which results in 2 total hits.  NATO assigns hits to Spanish surface and to Convoy-Med.  Spanish surface unit is flipped and 1 hit to Convoy-Med equates to two hits and a 2 marker is placed on it.  Cruise Missile Fired markers are placed on both Oscar SSGNs. NATO PhaseNATO plays one operation point to activate an Improved Los Angeles class submarine.  It moves into West 4-5 from West 6 to perform Antisubmarine Warfare.  A Soviet Yankee class SSN and a Soviet Yankee SSBN are in the First Strike area (West 6).  The Soviets roll 1D10 as First Strike evasion to try and evade the American SSN.  Soviets roll “1”.  Evasion roll fails.  The Improved Los Angeles performs an ASW die roll. NATO rolls 3D10 with +2 Tactical value.  NATO rolls 3, 10, and 10; which modify to 5, 12, and 12.  Resulting in 2 values high enough to cause hits on the Soviet submarines.  The two natural 10s allow the NATO player to assign the damage.  NATO player assigns both hits to SSBN sinking it; however, the Soviets play a reaction card “Double Hull/Clusterguard” which negates one successful attack leaving it damaged.  Due to previous operations and card play the Soviet hand drops to 2 cards so he immediately draws a card to bring him back to 3.

tier2.body: So one of the factors in the venerable Clancy/Bond book "Red Storm Rising" was that both US and Pact left the Pacific theater quiet in order to reinforce their battle in the Atlantic. In the Soviet case, I think it was mostly air assets pulled to Europe, and in the US case, it was reinforcing well into the war with CVNs and MAUs - sorry for any spoilers there... But if you haven't read that book and you are reading this thread, what on Earth are you waiting for?  What if there was a scenario where this is reversed?  That for whatever reason, the Soviets start hostilities with strategic reinforcement from Atlantic-dedicated formations?  That may create some interesting possibilities with the battle over Japan, Alaska, etc, since those largely-defensive Soviet units now have enough muscle to really go on the attack and surge out.  And depending, you might see additional US forces arriving as reinforcements as well.The con here is that this would surely involve additional counters, upping the game cost.  But the option of playing "vanilla Pacific" and "steroids Pacific" may add to the appeal of the title to justify additional costs. tier2.author: wedgeantilles1971
tier2.body: Some thoughts as something of a historian sitting in my comfortable armchair…  I’m making no claim to being an expert!  Just an avid amateur. And when I mentioned “US”, I’m also including partner nations and forces such as the UK, Australia, New Zealand, Canada, Japan, and South Korea in that term.  No convenient label like “NATO” I can apply here as a catch-all.It seems like the strategic Soviet goals circa 1987 would be something along the lines of:•	Keep their SSBNs safe, whether wandering around the Northern Pacific or tucked safely in their Okhotsk bastion.  A Soviet choice here could be to keep them safely grouped behind the heavy defenses along the Kurile Islands and Kamchatka where they can be protected with fewer assets.  Or, they could be risked by going on patrols into the Northern Pacific in order to shorten missile flight times and thus score some politically-aligned VPs.  But the risk of keeping most in the bastion is that they are now grouped up for any nervy US SSNs looking to sneak in among them.•	Maintain their major port of Vladivostock (and maybe Cam Rahn Bay after reading Edgar’s post).  Very much in line with Stuart’s mention of a “survive” goal – protect their infrastructure.  So this would be denying the Sea of Japan and South China Sea to US forces.  •	Maintain North Korea as a player in Pacific geopolitics.  This would largely involve interdicting convoys approaching South Korea.  And this is probably where the need to control the Sea of Japan and also suppress Japan’s western coast heavily enters into the equation.•	Degrade the US ability to project power throughout the Pacific.  I could see them scoring points for strikes on Subic Bay, Guam, Okinawa, and Alaska.  So it feels like the bar is somewhat low for the Soviets when defining “victory” and that I could see a lot of pressure on the US to go on the offensive and push into what would be contested waters and airspace to fulfill the objectives of defending Taiwan, Japan, South Korea, and the major island installations.

tier2.author: wedgeantilles1971
tier2.body: blindsey wrote: I'm not sure that the Soviet Union would have had the means to actually invade Japan, although I have no doubt they would have used naval forces to disrupt trade and supply between the US and Japan.  I would guess that the Soviets had plans for neutralizing the major facilities at both Yokosuka and Okinawa, but I'm not convinced they would have been able to pull off a full-scale invasion, at least not until they had managed to either defeat the US or fight NATO to a standstill.My understanding was that one of the likely scenarios would have been a Soviet invasion of Japan's northern island - Hokkaido. Hokkaido has seafront property on the Sea of Okhotsk and was something of a gap in the Soviet defense of their Sea of Okhotsk "boomer bastion". Although I think they probably would have been content with suppressing the airfields on Hokkaido in order to control or interdict the airspace to prevent P-3 Orions from sniffing around their bastion.But yeah, I never read about any plans for any intended landings on any of the other main islands of Japan.

tier2.author: Edgar
tier2.body: Stuart Tonge  @stuuk I agree that the Pacific fleet was designed for defence, and not sure why taking a convoy to Vietnam would be a thing the Soviets would have particularly wanted to do?Perhaps if the Vietnamese were fighting on land, or else to support Soviet planes already there - but I wouldn't have thought it the cornerstone of a Soviet Pacific strategy.As wiki says (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cam_Ranh_Bay): Cam Ranh is considered the finest deepwater shelter in Southeast Asia.Four years after the fall of Saigon and the unification of North and South Vietnam, Cam Ranh Bay became an important Cold War naval base for the Soviet Pacific Fleet.In 1979, the Soviet government signed an agreement with Vietnam for a 25-year lease of the base. Cam Ranh Bay was the largest Soviet naval base outside the Soviet Union, allowing it to project increased power in the East Sea.[citation needed] by 1987, they had expanded the base to four times its original size and often made mock attacks in the direction of the Philippines, according to intelligence of the United States Pacific Fleet[citation needed]. Analysts suggested that the Vietnamese side also saw the Soviet presence there as a counterweight against any potential Chinese threat. The Soviet Union and Vietnam officially denied any presence there. However, as early as 1988, then-Soviet foreign minister Eduard Shevardnadze had discussed the possibility of a withdrawal from Cam Ranh Bay, and concrete naval reductions were realised by 1990.If you want to go there, and the Chinese government is not going to allow your forces pass through their country, the only way is by sea. Convoys are most needed to supply the base, and to send troops to defend it (or other tasks).It's likely an important naval base, and well situated for the USSR. You can't count on China joining your side on a war, they could have been neutral (or doing their own war against Taiwan, or dealing with one or both sides to have them not interfering).

tier3.author: Rick
tier3.body: Attacks on land targets by aircraft - whether bombing or using cruise - are always opposed by CAP in the base.There are essentially two modes of air combat in the game:- Interception takes place when strikes get hit *on the way* to the target. In this hypothetical that would mean fighters which have been placed On Patrol in either the Norwegian Sea or North 9-10. There's also an edge case where exiting an area with a carrier in let's it do interception, but if the US has a carrier in North 9-10 the Soviets really have other problems.- CAP is done *at the destination* by any fighters present. Carriers can CAP themselves, other taskforces in the same zone, or land bases IF they're in the specific zone the attack comes in through. So again in your hypothetical - the RAF fighters can come up. Saratoga in East 6 can't assist because the attack isn't coming via East 6, but could have if it was in the Norwegian Sea.The tactical dilemma between the two is, basically, that interception hits a lot harder but is easier to dodge. CAP is generally less lethal but by dint of being at the target - impossible to dodge if you want to strike it.Interception usually loses a dice from the fighters going on patrol, but in return strike craft get no save against interception. There's also the fact that detection by interceptors gives a bonus to subsequent CAP. Working through an example attack on the UK....- if all 3 RAF units are on CAP - that's a lot of CAP dice, but you get a 6+ save against all of them. Also you can fly straight past the UK to attack the shipping lanes. - so let's put a fighter on patrol over East 6 to protect the shipping lanes. Good but - if the Soviets decide to attack the UK, they'll come via the Norwegian Sea and that fighter will be out of position. We'll just get a 2 unit CAP.- so let's get another fighter up over North 5-6. Now we're cooking - on either of the obvious approaches they'll have to chance interception. However....- a Soviet player who is willing to risk his Bear-G (doubtful STAVKA noises) could still fly North 9-10 - East 9-10 - East 5 - East 3 - East 4 - and attack the UK that way! Now two of your fighters are out of position, and you've got a single CAP unit

tier3.author: Caustizer
tier3.body: In the full campaign, it's wise as the Soviets to use the "starting" Submarine placements to set up diesel subs with high dice counts versus convoys in mid-ocean spaces beyond the SOSUS line if you can. Foxtrots are nice for this, as it puts them in a position where they can start attacking NATO convoys early in the game. If you use these placements on Nuclear submarines, expect your diesel subs to struggle to be useful for a big chunk of the game as they are slow and have a hard time penetrating the SOSUS line. Take advantage of bad weather when you can to try and slip your missile submarines through the SOSUS line!

tier3.author: undaunted
tier3.body: 17.4 Types of air to air combatWhen Interception or CAP attacks occur they are resolved depending on what the triggering unit is:...If the unit triggering is a Fighter unit use ‘Fighter vs Fighter’17.6 Fighter vs FighterIf both sides have fighters in the same Sea Zone the Soviet player must declare if he will avoid combat followed by the NATO player...17.6 seems to contradict 17.4, whereas in 17.6 it seems to say fighter to fighter combat occurs whenever both sides have fighters present in the zone, while 17.4 put FvF under the framework of interception and CAP.https://boardgamegeek.com/thread/2559101/cap-and-interceptio...Base on the second example (w/ Tornados and Phantom escorts vs. Foxbats on patrol and carrier Yak, it seems like the 17.4 is the correct interpretation.If the zone has two fighters on patrol, entering the zone triggers interception.If the zone has two carrier fighters, entering the zone does not trigger interception.  Leaving the zone triggers carrier fighter interception, or alternatively, performing a mission in the zone (eg., the intruding enemy fighter go on patrol) will trigger CAP.If the zone has one fighter on patrol and one carrier fighter, then an enemy fighter entering the zone will trigger FvF interception from the fighter on patrol, and if the enemy fighter go on patrol, it triggers FvF CAP.Maybe 17.6 only means that when both sides have fighters in zone, FvF interception and FvF CAP are mandatory, so combat is avoided only when one side bug out?  For example, if the zone has one fighter on patrol and one carrier fighter, and an enemy fighter the zone to go on patrol there, what could happen is that entering the zone triggers FvF interception by the fighter on the patrol, let's say the fighter on patrol decides to avoid combat and RTB spent, then the enemy fighter goes on patrol and trigger FvF CAP by the carrier fighter, and let's say this time both side decide to fight it out.Another interesting situation is say 1x Phantom is on patrol and 1x carrier Tomcat on an adjacent zone, and 1x Foxbats + 1x Flogger move from the zone w/ carrier to zone w/ Phantom, would it trigger a single 2v2 interception or two separate 1v1 interceptions?

Just that other games seem to be prioritized, when I run into these problems.I have just received the game and using Gomez's advice 1,1a,2,2a - also reading through the session reports between game sessions.IMO the biggest hurdle to assimilating the rules is they are designed as a reference but the play aids do not reference them, which I have attempted to remedy by posting a Play Aid chart reference, I also labelled up the physical rules with the errata R# and C# clarifications as relevant, which was packaged with the game on cardstock. The first 5 scenarios plus variants form a programmed learning and are fun but winning isn't their aim, learning how effective the weapon systems and counter measures are one system at a time is their priority.In play I work from the Actions and Turn Sequence play aid , The main clarifications needed from the off is for the Turn Sequence Ships Event.Quote:A useful clarification to the QRS Action and Turn sequence card for Ships 1) read all the "," as or :-1) All TFs may move one Sea Zone or resolve ASW or mark 'landing' or land if already markedThe left column effectively provides actions available outside of turn events and cards supplement these. Like any new game Analysis Paralysis can set in but scenarios 1-5 are the cure. Scenario 1 - USSR is waiting on NATO and NATO IS waiting on USSR - as they stare each other out it becomes contagious, this is an opportunity to test who blinks, send out on patrol subs and MP , move some NATO subs to the arctic, attack some Subs in the Norwegian Sea. Form a USSR task force. You know the USSR won't sortie North of SOSUS until NATO attack their boomers until they do the action will be jockeying for position, sending a few shots across the bows. Situation at the end of turn 1 scenario 1Looking at the situation I decide I want to I want to make a Sub move and attack, from the Play aid Actions and Turn Sequence, I labelled CF(Cyan Front) top left column... then using the table reference , I keep in the Rules as "Page 1" , the rules for subs is at 16.2 and the play aid for them is BF(Blue Front) and the rules sections for Sub actions are 17.8 etc  . After a few turns I found that worked quite well and rarely need to refer to the rulebook for actions I had taken a few times, just the play aid tables. I intend to create a pictorial play aid cross referencing the play aids , hence devising this system.By the end of Scenario 1 I was looking at the optional rules (the Die/DRM impacts are on the play aids) and for 1a using the cards for Reactions(only a few will apply, but they refresh each turn).

tier3.author: Nicolas
tier3.body: Stuart Tonge  @stuuk Hmm the Brest issue is interesting. I assumed there would be enough ports / infrastructure in each area with a convoy port to handle unloading tasks, but I don't honestly recall whether I did a thorough study on that. It's also possible I confused port updates made more recently than the 1980's.Brest is purely a military base.  It must have some minor unloading capacity but even Saint Malo and Saint Nazaire probably have more .... but, beyond that, the main problem is the lack of good connections to the rail & road network, which is nothing like the one between Le Havre & Paris (and then on to Belgium or Germany). The French Western seaboard, in 1985, is really far from Paris - 591 km - (today there are TGVs for passenger transport but they don't go all the way at high speed).  The road capacity is also not that good (2 x 2 motorways at best, with little redundancy).  The only two ports that really have the capacity to efficiently unload a convoy and get the contents moving are Le Havre, which has excellent rail, road & river connections to Paris and from there to the rest of the country, and, to a lesser extent, Marseille / La Ciotat.  Hence my idea to add one hit (could even be 2) to convoys landing there (which does require NATO to land its convoys further into the Channel - this can balance additional French ships or subs :-D).

tier3.author: Darth
tier3.body: Okay, to make some mess about the OoB of the Soviet Navy of the time:1. The Kara Group should be in the Med instead of Kresta (the Karas always served in the Black Sea Fleet) and it should have SAM = 5 (for it had an Azov CG with same SA-N-6 system as on Slava cruiser - Azov being test ship for that system) - and the Provorny DDG too - test ship for SA-N-7 system; it could be upgraded to have 3 launchers, thus being sort of a Sovremenny in that group).You could alternatively add Provorny to Moscow/Leningrad CVGH group, to have it SAM value = 1.2. Slava cruiser:In fact the “Slava” cruiser has served from the very beginning (and serves today, as “Moskva”), in the Black Sea Fleet. The “Imp. Slava” (in fact “Marshal Ustinov”, recently upgraded) has always served (and still does) in the Northern Fleet.Thus IMHO it should be added as part of - and replace the counter - one of the Sov-Udaloy groups (either the basic one or “85+”):a) if replaces the “old” group, then should have: 4 SAM, 3 red SSMs, 4 white SSMs, 2 black SSMs, 4 ASW, R (rocket torpedoes)b) if replaces the “new 85+” group, then should have: 5 SAM, 3 red SSMs, 3 white SSMs, 2 black SSMs, 4 ASW, R (rocket torpedoes)And this also means that Slava should be in the Med Squadron too.This would, unfortunately, make the Baltic and Northern Fleets weaker, but, well, at least they would be augmented by adding 1 Slava to their existing units (single Slava cruiser is worth, as counting the values, 1 ASW, 1 SAM and 2 black SSMs).However, there should be added another Sverdlov-class cruiser to the Northern Fleet (Murmansk and her sister-ship).3. IMVHO in case the Soviets pull "Turkish neutrality" option, they should also get a third Sverdlov-class cruiser (Mikhail Kutuzov and her sister ships from the Black Sea) anywhere on the map, plus an additional amphib and 1 troops counter (Black Sea Naval Infantry plus transport, released by the Turkish hospitality).4. Another option:if the Soviets pull "Turkish neutrality" option, then the Kutuzov and Med Amphib could be available for amphib landing on Crete or Malta, with the Iceland rules being applied.BTW: how do you place the Badgers in the Med? They would have to overfly Turkey, as the Iran-Iraq-Syria route is too long...

tier3.author: Herr
tier3.body: We are BIG fans of Cold War goes Hot in god's country (and Gotham city). Been playing games in this genre since back in the day (mid 80s). One favorite is   : I was lucky enough to play two complete campaigns (all four modules) with my   mate Steve K. Yeah; we dig WW3 games in Minnesota...and NYCIn particular,   Designer Frank Chadwick gave us the cards that   built upon in   . Two decades later, I took the idea and ran with it in  Back to WW3 designs...A few years ago on   , we did an episode on Cold War Goes Hot: Episode XVI: July 31, 2013. A survey of games then:Updated...I believe we now have another fine addition to this genre: Blue Water Navy: The War at SeaA dear gaming mate, JR, and I gave it go in early March 2021. Our good friend Bob H also popped in. We had a practice session, that witnessed JR's Soviets partying in Reykjavík. We later determined that we had made a few mistakes. Bitten by the BWN bug, we immediately set up to play the 1983 campaign game. Following is a session report. First, a bit about the game...From our first go. Soviet wet dream in Iceland. It never happened. It is a rumor. A specter. An echo of what might have been. Lesson: When the Soviet leads with the "Paratroop" Card, BEWARE! Respond and NEVER lose the land of Björk Guðmundsdóttir as NATO.  Sugarcubes en vivo 19/20: VitaminPlayIn simpler times {the Cold War}...Pre COVID/Putin/Trump...there was live music, parties and free love in Moskva, NYC, MPLS and Reykjavík.So, What's in the Box?A pile of stuff. Rulebook (more on that $#$#$%^@% thing below), Playbook, nice looking counters, some somewhat helpful playaids and a decent double map (mandatory for a beefy wargame...well, a few exceptions: ex:   ,   , etc.Before discussing components, let's talk a bit about the design....A Labour of Love...Smart Design...Innovative...Right Scale...Full of FlavorIt is wonderfully clear, this is a labour of love. My favorite type:  first time designers biting off WAY more than they can chew. This is middleweight beast: 20 hours for a campaign game (estimated)...complex (but, not really).. a ton of sub game systems...many interlocking parts. Ample decent and beloved chrome (god bless these two designers). You can see where it checks vs other high rated heavy/beefy wargames here: A bit about how it all fits together:Turn and Stability track1) Card > Ops > Impulses: At its heart, cards generate OPs points that you then spend to do stuff. I Pulse, then You Pulse. Primarily, you spend these OPs points on an action with an asset and/or to play events (many events have a cost to play).2) Segregation of Large Forces and Assets: Movement of task forces occurs at particular points on the OPs Track ("impulse track"). Very smart. 3) Right feel/scale: This mix - of individual asset action and task force action - really captures modern combat well (hell, it could be applied to any op strategic game). Essentially armies (in this case navies/air forces) and heroes battling it out at different points in the turn. I'm a sucker for op strategic games and this one delivers.War tracksSoviet Stability track4) Decent level of abstraction and interplay of dynamics impacting the conflict: A number of game tracks that interact with game developments controlled by actions of the players reflect the dimensions of this hypothetical conflict. Of course, no one knows what all the dynamics would have been, but, the designers took a decent stab at it.I love strategic will tracks. Essentially, there is one here: The Soviet Stability Track: a way to make the Soviets go wobbly. War tracks solve the problem of not having part of the game deal with detailed land ops. You want that? Try   The Air and Naval operations in Blue Water Navy impact the progress of the Soviet blitz of the West. Well handled by the designers.Sample card5) Card assisted: Cool cards that generate OPS points and various capabilities for each player6) Air and Naval rules ALWAYS suck...but, not here: Detailed, but not ridiculous, resolution of naval and air combat systems.Back to components...As you can see from this counter description chart, a lot of stuff. All good, but, not overwhelming. Yes, you need to frequently check the counter key for info, until you've played it enough.Ok...the rulebook and playaids (prepare the fire). We had a number of issues:1) Not contained in one section All the bits pertaining to a particular game component were not contained in the same section.2) No effective cross referencing:  The playaids do NOT reference the appropriate rules section. This drove us nuts.3) Organization. The rulebook thwarts one from diving in and pushing counters: at least we hardcore wargamers (EiA, ASL, WiF, etc.) were.We did NOT find the rules unclear (once we found the particular rule), loosely written, in conflict with other sections or nonsensical. No, the issue is identified above: organization/cross referencing. Fixable.The game does need an up to date FAQ and errata sheet: hopefully the designer and/or a cheerleader can step in.There are a PILE (100's) of rules threads, but, not that far out of the ordinary for a complex, beefy wargame that is getting a lot of play (see table below) - BWN leads the pack by a bit in terms of rules threads relative to all threads...I'm guessing that is due the three items stated above...pilgrims lost in the rulebook somewhere[/b]The designer (Stuart) provides OUTSTANDING support for his game. So, you got a question? Search for it...don't see it? - post it.So, how did we get over the rulebook hump? We watched the OUTSTANDING playthru videos here of BGG. We read a few good session reports. I also put together a one page (double sided) playaid {if one complains, one needs to try to solve the problem}. Link to it below. And, MOST IMPORTANTLY, we jumped into the deep end of the campaign game. No other way to tame a beast. None. So, on to a recap of our session...http://talk.consimworld.com/WebX?233@@.1dcfcaab!enclosure=.1... Day 1: First Blood...the Race for PositionBob H, JR, me pushing counters and tossing dice via Vassal and Skype during COVID: On this particular day, we are blessed.Cards: Soviet: “Politburo” 12 Ops, NATO: “Italian Air Strike” 12Early Day one: First contactD1S1 (Day 1, Soviet first impulse): Soviets target N56 (region North 5-6) for Sub hunting. Ineffective.D1N1: Seeing the threat to Norway, NATO sends an Orion to N910 (Barent Sea) to detect the Soviet aggressors…TF (task force) detected…a “good” detection results. NATO is pleased.D1S2: Soviets conduct a sub attack in N56…a miss.D1N2: NATO now launches a sub attack on the TF in the Barent Sea. Evading soviet defenses, a big fat torpedo finds it mark in the Kynda Group of escorts: a cheer goes out! Soviets blinded by the explosion miss with their ASW response.NATO opens the action with a patrolNATO attacks a Soviet TFEarly Day one: Soviet SurgeD1S3: Soviets use card event to SURGE four predatory subs into N78(1), N56(1), N910 (2). A kilo finds a NATO Churchill class subs and hits it.D1N3: NATO responds by reinforcing N910 (Barents Sea) with another sub.D1S4: Soviets begin building a bearpack under the artic cap with a couple of boomers.D1N4: NATO dispatches another Orion on patrol in N78 (Sea zone NE of Iceland)At this point, we hit “8” on the Ops track, time for all FAST TFs to move (unless in poor weather…they get a 1 turn delay). This is an outstanding game mechanic – where the fleets only move during a couple of points in the turn, while individual assets (planes, subs almost exclusively) move during the rest of the turn. It captures, well, the tempo of modern combat. No reason it could not be utilized in non-modern strategic operational scale games.Mid Day one: JR’s Soviet Sea of Sorrows (aka the North Sea) begins…D1S5: Soviets send a sub on patrol at N34…which would later be known as “JR’s Soviet Sea of Sorrows”….D1N5: The dutch sub, Zwaardvis, sails for glory to N34…attacks a soviet sub and plants a big fat fish into its side. The Dutch rejoice.D1S6: Soviets reinforces the bearpack under the artic cap with 2 more subs.D1N6: NATO forms TF at Devenport.Day 1 Post "5" Ships“5” SHIPs on the Ops Track occurs. All TF move (except those suffering poor weather – they get a turn delay).Late Day one: Positioning for day 2D1S7: Soviet send sub on patrol in N34 (the North Sea)D1N7: NATO hunts boomer in W45…unsuccessfullyD1S8: Soviet send sub on patrol in N34D1N8: NATO dispatches LA class sub to N910…Soviets intercept and a Tango finds and sadly kills it first sub: a LA class. An inquiry will be made.Comments: We loved "the build up". Great op strategic wargames all have "the build up"...the marshaling of forces, getting into position and awaiting (or precipitating) the first big clash. The whole first turn was "the build up". Soviets have the initiative and forces NATO to respond. NATO is trying to use its ops to parry the thrust and invest somewhere in prep for the next few days. Great tension. As NATO, I constantly struggled with "here is what I want to do and here is what I must do...NOW". Impulse angst.Day 2: JR's Sea of Soviet Sorrows, a BIG ARSE Bearpack under the Arctic and a bombs rain on soviet tanks in So EuropeCard played on Day 1 and Day 2Cards: Soviet: “Paratroop” 15 Ops, NATO: “Eagles” 12 Ops…since we ended day on 3rd space on Ops track, each side adjusts their ops to 17 for Soviets and 14 for NATOEarly Day 2: JR’s Soviet Sea of Sorrows [N34] claims many Russian lads.D2S1: Soviet reinforce bearpack under the articD2N1: Orion dispatched to W45 to hunt boomers….fails to sink the beast.D2S2: Soviet send a flying bear to detect TF Delta in N78. Poor detection achievedD2N2: PassD2S3: Soviet send a flying bear to detect TF Delta in N78. Good detection achievedNOTE: We determined that we had forgotten to conduct Danish mine attacks on soviet subs crossing the Danish straits Day 1. So, we rolled dice…3 hits out of 3! One soviet sub sunk, two damaged.JR's Sea of Soviet SorrowsD2N3: NATO LA class sub runs to N78: Soviets miss an interceptionD2S4: Another Soviet sub sorties to N34…another danish mine does it job…4 for 4 on mine rolls. Danes rejoice…again!D2N4: PassD2S5: Another Soviet sub sorties to N34…another danish mine does it job…5 for 5 on mine rolls. Danes rejoice…again! JR curses the Danes and begins an counter intel investigation.D2N5: Nimrod dispatched to N56 goes on patrolD2S6: ASW attacks by furious soviet helo’s in N910. Unfortunate Norwegian sub explodes: Olso is sad.Boomer hunting can be funMid Day 2: A shift away from the North Atlantic to other fronts…Soviet artic bearpack growsD2N6: More boomer hunting in W45. Ineffective againNOTE: Soviets receive “first strike points” if they can maintain sufficient boomer payload in spaces off USA coast.D2S7: And yet another soviet sub led by a fool decides to sortie to N34…Danes incredible mines respond…die rolled…BAM! 6 for 6. Premier JR gets out his abacus and calculates 6 for 6 hits with Danish mines are a 4 out 1000 chance. The Danes shout, “Damm your odds!”D2N7: TF Lightning formed at Norfolk.D2S8: Soviets send a sub to N78 to patrolD2N8: TF Ranger formed in Spain…planning a trip to the warm Med…to make things warmer for the Soviet tanks rolling into to Southern Europe.Check out (click on the image) that bear pack in the Arctic...and E910 (East 9-10)!Arctic BearpackIcelandic FrontComments. Yes, NATO is getting worried by the bear pack in the Arctic and the one in E910. Day 3 & 4 could be soviet hammer time.D2S9: Soviets send another sub to N78 to patrolD2N9: LA class sub from Norfolk hunts boomer in W45…finds it…hits both it and its escort.D2S10: More soviet subs to the artic bearpackD2N10: NATO sends a sub from Norfolk to E5D2S11: Soviets send bombers from Kola to strike TFDelta. US-5 ship sinks (only ship in this decoy TF).D2N11: Another LA from Norfolk goes boomer hunting in W45. Two soviets subs sink in warm waters of the Caribbean. D2S12: More soviet subs to the artic bearpack…NATO begins to worry about where this horde is going Day 3…D2N12: PassNATO strikes soviet tanks in So EuropeNATO Strike force returns to TF Ranger. And celebrate.Late Day 2: Day 2 closes with bombing run on soviets forces in Southern EuropeD2S13: Soviets send sub into N78. A LA class sub notches other soviet sub victim. D2N13: NATO dispatches sub to M89D2S14: Soviet sub hunts in N78. See nothing but some floating garbage.“5” SHIPs on the Ops Track occurs. All TF move. Soviets deploy amphibs off of coast of Norway.D2N14: PassD2S15: Soviet sub sorties to N78 and is promptly sunk by patrolling NATO asset.D2N15: PassD2S16: Soviet sub sorties to N78D2N16: NATO launches a strike on Soviet TF Bordino off coast of Norway. NATO missiles find a target: Soviet escort sunk.D2S17: Soviet sub sorties to E910D2N17: TF Ranger in west Med launches a strike on soviet tank columns in Southern Europe. BIG SUCCESS! 3 hits achieved which will delay soviet advancement on the So Europe War Track.D2S18: Soviets end turn with subs going to E910 and N78. Soviets manage to find a LA class NATO sub. However, captain has is lucky charm, uses it, and successfully makes a save roll. Day 2 ends.Comments: Who the hell knows if NATO or the Soviet player has the edge. NATO was real happy out Soviet sub losses in the Sea of Sorrows, hunting here and there and taking out the boomers near the USA. Preventing the So Europe War Track from advancing was a real win. And, the weather delaying the invasion of Norway. However, Premier JR is wise. He has positioned a sh*tload of subs (including boomers) in the arctic and North Atlantic for Day 3 & 4 foolishness.Day 2 end of turnWrap up: TWO BIG THUMBS UPA sad day for Soviet subs in the North Sea..Leningrad Cowboys - Happy TogetherPlayBack in the day...   ...AAR:  Tracking Sheet from VG's Fleet Series...not needed with Blue Water Navy: you don't need to keep track of pastaGreat gameplay. At least, that's our view so far. It produces a hell of a story line.No idea if it is balanced, and, we could care less. Yes, burn the rule book. Check out the VERY good video's here on BGG. Read the rules (prior to burning). Jump in. You'll figure it out. At least, close enough.Mates have asked me, "Is it like Victory Games Fleet series". No: BWN is MUCH less complex (the game weight indicated WAY too high: this is NOT a complex game...it just has a lot of parts and rulebook makes it much worse than necessary) and benefits from the last 3 decades of game design. I can see the lineage, but, this not the Fleet series. Two different systems. Big tip of the hat to the designers. This game has landed in rarified air:   VERY few wargames have a game weight above 4.0 AND a high game rating. Even fewer from first time designers; you count them on a few paws. Consequently, JR and I will be at Day 3 soon. Can't wait.So, if you like WW3 storyline, take a load off and get this game. Get on Vassal. Play it.Link to other 1st MN/Sawatdee/Herr Dr AARs:

tier3.author: LeSpass
tier3.body: Yes and yes. From what I understand, there is no submarine vs submarine combat like the fighter vs fighter combat where both sides roll dice and cause step loss simultaneously.For ASW, the player decides to use one action to hunt subs on a particular Sea Zone with a unit that can perform that action (it cannot attack a particular unit, that is decided on step loss allocation after the roll). Then it rolls to decide the results of the hunt. The action is complete and the unit is spent.If the enemy submarine wants to roll to attack the unit that just performed the ASW, it has to do the same thing during its player's turn.There are very particular exceptions to this rule. (See Shkval torpedo and SSBN hunting)So for example, in the case of the video. Soviet would use the Echo or the Juliet to perform ASW ops on the Norway Sea. The Los Angeles would react and attack the moving sub for entering the Sea Zone because it is 'On Patrol'. After the Los Angeles has performed its reaction, the Echo or Juliet would then conduct ASW operations in the area. If the Los Angeles was not 'On Patrol', it would have to wait to its player's turn to perform ASW.If the Echo and Juliet go for missile coordination, the Los Angeles would roll ASW for being 'On Patrol' and then damage allocation rules decide how the step losses go. Afterwards, Echo and Juliet attack the land facility with missiles.I hope I didn't make it more confusing.

tier3.author: MattD123
tier3.body: So we played this on Friday....We finished 6 turns..at that point we called it as a NATO win. Total time was 12 hours but that included set up and some interuptions for food, people coming over and asking questions etc.The first turn especially was long as we learned rules and also there is so much to do that initial ops are quite hard to prioritise. Turns definitely got faster as we got up to speed and had plans in mind etc. I think realistically it's going to be about a 12 hour game for the full game next time.We both had great fun ... we ran into a few rules questions but it was easy enough to just agree to do something that felt right. The game was well paced...lots of stuff going on and less and less chart referal as we went on. We both made lots of tactical errors....and learned a lot about both sides capabilities in the game.Soviets got close to winning but then NATO got a big TF (2 convoys) through and played the counterattack card...which stopped them. Soviets had lost almost ALL their attack subs by then....NATO would have hunted down the additional boomer or 2 they needed to collapse the USSR for sure before the soviets could advance again in Europe.ThanksMatt

tier3.body: Thanks so much for posting the AAR. I have played this scenario a couple of times (solo), still trying to get up to speed on the game system (both sides winning once). I solo a lot of games, but this one seems to really demand the "spirit" of head-to-head gaming. It's not nearly as fun solo as I thought it would be, but A LOT more fun with an opponent than I imagined. And after it's all said and done, gaming WWIII had better be fun if you are going to commit hours to the campaign game. I really admire the system, it basically plays like VITP on steroids and other PEDs. Area movement, buckets of dice, and differentiated weapon systems, exponentially more complex but nevertheless satisfying. And  let's not forget, rolling dice and kicking ass is the prevalent theme in most "fun" wargames. Like I said, it screams for a live opponent...I know it can be disheartening to publish an AAR and have others point out your mistakes. Your courage is laudable.  Please don't be discouraged. Many of us benefitted from your mistakes, but more importantly from your detailed write-up. It was great! Hopefully you will continue on through the scenarios and share them with us, which will help us to grasp the game. Salut!

tier3.author: Eldard
tier3.body: A few comments on Soviet Navy operations in the Arctic and, Atlantic in the early '80s.1 - Soviet Strategic Bastion:  The primary mission of the Soviet Navy was strategic nuclear attack.  This was vested in its Yankee-class, Delta-classes, and the new Typhoon-class SSBNs Generally, the Soviets maintained 2 Yankees on patrol off the US East (and 2 more off the West Coast).  They needed to be close enough for the range of their SS-N-6 SLBMs, but this left them vulnerable to US SSNs bird-dogging them in cat-and-mouse games at all times.  The Delta-IVs and new Typhoons (SS-N-20) had the range to strike CONUS from a "bastion" in the Arctic Circle where they could be protected by land-based air units as well as surface vessels.  The fear was that NATO naval units would penetrate the bastion and destroy the SSBNs (the Soviet strategic nuclear reserve) before they could be used.2 - Soviet Submarine Barriers:  The Soviet Northern Fleet would deploy Foxtrot SSs, Victor SSNs, and Charlie SSGNs in concentric barriers from the homeland toward the GIUK Gap.  The objective was to deter USN carrier battle groups (CVBGs) from getting close enough to the USSR to launch nuclear air strikes.  Once detected, the US CVBGs would also be attacked by entire regiments of Soviet Naval Aviation Tu-16/Badgers and Tu22M/Backfires, simultaneously launching long range ASMs at the carriers to saturate USN missile defenses. (It was this threat that inspired the production of the US F-14/Tomcat and its long-range AIM-66/Phoenix AAM in the '70s to shoot down the enemy aircraft before they reached their launch point.)  3 - Soviet Amphibious Landings:  These would be used to advance down the Norwegian coast primarily in support of Soviet army advances, and to seize NATO airfields for both denial to NATO and forward deployment of Soviet land-based strike, ASW, and recon aircraft.4 - SLOC Interdiction:  The lowest priority of the Soviet Northern Fleet was interdiction of NATO sea lines of communication (SLOC) between North America and Europe. NATO did fear the mining of NATO ports, so the majority of NATO MCM capability resided with the European members.  The Soviet Baltic Fleet:  The primary mission of this fleet was to protect the right flank of the Soviet and WP ground offensive as it advanced, launching amphibious landings as appropriate to support that advance. It consisted of mainly older Soviet Navy vessels.A word about Keflavik:  This was NATO's unsinkable aircraft carrier.  Fighters like the USAF F-15/Eagle, E-3A/AWACS aircraft, and USN ASW/maritime patrol P-3/Orion were expected to patrol the GIUK Gap and seas north in support of the advancing NATO strike groups and SSNs.

tier3.author: Dodo98
tier3.body: NATO ACTIONOPs 9 > 8, Nato sends some P3 Orion from Bermuda on an ASW patrol, to cover TF Aegis.SOVIET ACTIONMiG 31 from Kola on Patrol over the Barents sea, with the intention of intercepting likely Nato air strikes against the invasion TF and the Kola bases. OPs 9 > 8FAST EVENTBoth sides OP markers have now reached the Fast event so it is triggered. Only 2 Task Forces are eligible to move, TF Hammer and Viking, but only TF Hammer moves a zone, from Mid 5 to East 3. TF Viking stays in the Baltic sea. NATO ACTIONThe Thresher submarines lurking in the waters around Jamaica pick up several new submerged contacts. After a short time, the contacts are confirmed to be several Yankee class submarines, including probably also SSBNs. Immediately the hunting starts, but first the Soviets get their first strike evasion roll. A 3 is rolled, not enough to get away. So the Treshers attack with 3D10 + 1 DRM. 6, 8 and 10. Two step losses are caused, the soviets select the escorting SSNs for the first hit and Nato selects the SSBNs for the second hit. A very successful engagement for the Nato, with several enemy subs sunk including valuable SSBNs with a total payload of 2. OPs 8 > 7SOVIET ACTIONMeanwhile up in the north, several ASW helicopters are sent on patrol to further increase the ASW defense of their TF. OPs 8 > 7NATO ACTIONOPs 7 > 5, TF Ranger is formed at NAS Rota, consisting of some Sturgeons, the carriers Kitty Hawk and Kennedy and the Ships Groups 5 and 6. This very strong formation will set course towards Italy to support the fighting there with air strikes.SOVIET ACTIONSome Foxtrot submarines have picked up the location of TF Hammer in zone East 3 and move closer to start an attack.3D10(4 base dice -> +1 for Good detection on TF, -2 because diesel subs attacking a fast TF): 1, 3 and 4. No hits scored, so the submarines failed to move into an attack position and the TF escapes. OPs 7 > 6REPAIR EVENT1 hit is removed from the UK bases but they are still lightly damaged.

tier3.author: Dodo98
tier3.body: SOVIET ACTIONThe soviets have decided that it is of the utmost importance to damage the UK Air Fields to secure their marines in the Barents Sea against possible air strikes. So the High Command authorizes a second, division-strength, air strike this time with 3 Badger regiments from the Baltic. OPs 12>9. The Badgers will be escorted over Denmark by a regiment of MiG 25s. As soon as they reach the vicinity of Copenhagen, a danish squadron of F16 Falcons intercepts the strike. 3D10 for the danish fighters, they roll 5, 8, 9. With their +1 DRM, this is good enough for 2 hits on the escorting MiGs, which means that the complete regiment has been annihilated over Denmark. Not a good start to this mission for the soviets.. As the strike has now been detected, it's a risky move to continue but the soviets need those bases damaged, so they continue nonetheless. Next up is the CAP from the 2 F4s at the Scottish bases. They each get 4 dice (+1 because strike is detected) and their DRM. Modified rolls: 4, 8, 8, 10 and 3, 4, 6, 11. That's four hits (the N10 would mean this kill takes place before the missile launch). But first the Badgers get a save throw against each hit, a 6+ cancels the hit. Results are: One 8 and the N10 were not canceled. So those two hits remain and are applied.Because the N10 killed a step before launch, "only" 15 missiles are now in the air. 3D10: 3, 7, 8. The 3 is a miss but the 7 and the 8 each cause 1 hit and 1 kill. The soviets select the Buccaneers for the first kill and the NATO selects a Nimrod squadron for the second. 2 hits are placed on the facility which means it's now lightly damaged, so no air units can fly for the moment and the F4 on patrol has to return and is marked spent.The attack was quite acceptable in the end. It could have been better, but also worse.Next time, we'll see how the NATO reacts to those losses, stay tuned.

tier3.author: Dodo98
tier3.body: Optional rulesI use the ones recommended by the designer in the rulebook.Turn 1 / Day 1CONVOY PLACEMENTThe Nato places a SAM Convoy at Norfolk. REINFORCEMENTS/OPERATIONSThe Soviets play a card worth 15 OPs with the OP event "KGB Assasinations".Nato plays a card worth 12 OPs with the event "SURTASS"SOVIET ACTIONNext up is the first soviet action of the war. They decide to strike the UK AFs with a 3 regiment Backfire attack, to suppress the RAF units there, especially the Buccaneer squadron, which could cause trouble to the soviet invasion TF. OPs 15>12. Over the Norwegian sea they are intercepted by the on patrol F4 squadron.The F4s roll with 2 dice (-1 die because they are intercepting). The rolls are: 1 and 6. Even with the +1 DRM from their Tactical value that is not good enough to kill something. Next, the 2 F4 squadrons left at the AFs fly their CAP mission.Both units are allowed to roll with all 3 dice + their DRM. Modified rolls are: 4,8,8 and 4,5,9. Bad day for the RAF pilots as they don't manage to shoot down a single Backfire. That means big trouble for the Air Fields as there are now 18 Missiles (144 in the real world) in the air. Looking at the Cruise Missile vs. Land Targets table, that gives the soviets 3 dice to roll: 1,2,3. Unbelievable but not a single missile hits a target, instead they end up in the sea or damage the surrounding cities, but the strategic important AFs remain 100% operational. For this failure, a nice resettlement to Siberia will await these pilots after their return...NATO ACTIONThe Nato will use it's Operation Event, which grants 4 ASW dice + the DRM of the selected unit to attack soviet submarines in a zone south of the GUIK gap. OPs 12>10. Nato chooses the Churchill group in East 6. Modified Rolls: 2,7,7,8. Only 1 hit scored against the Yankee SSN. The Yankee is flipped and the Churchill is spent.For it's other non-event action, Nato sends a british Nimrod squadron into the same zone to perform ASW. OPs 10>9.3D10: 2,3,6. No hits scored, Nimrod returns and is spent.That's it for now, if you spot any errors or have any other comments feel free to post them.

tier3.author: Dodo98
tier3.body: Hello Folks,This is my first attempt to write an AAR for a game, so bear with me if it's not perfect I decided to choose the 83' Standard Campaign (Tactical Surprise) because it has less units compared to the other campaigns, thus making it easier for solo play. For this campaign I will use the soviet solo bot which was uploaded by the designer to the files section here on BGG. I am interested to see how this works out and what effects it has on the course of the game. So, without further ado let's get started.All units have been set up according to the scenario book, so the next step is the:Pre-Game ChecklistNATO1. The NATO decides to breakdown a US Sturgeon from Norfolk and split the resulting 2 counters between TF Mustang and TF Black, thus enhancing their ASW capability immensely. 2. The Dutch ship group is sent to Kiel to later form a TF there with the germans ships. The purpose behind this redeployment is to immediately pressurize a possible Soviet TF there with the huge number of anti-ship missiles those groups carry. The second move involves the transfer from US-4 to TF Mustang (from TF Hammer). The intention here is to secure the valuable convoy against possible backfire attacks with additional SAM capacities.3. Now the previously mentioned TF consisting of the German and Dutch group is formed and placed in the Baltic Sea.4. For the 3 available submarine movements NATO selects the following boats: An UK Oberon to North 3-4, a French Daphne to East 4 and a US Thresher to W 2-3. The Oberon is assigned to guard the Gap between the UK and Norway against any soviet submarine intrusion attempt. The Daphne's primary task is the protection of the convoy lane to the french ports and the Tresher has the task to hunt for soviet boomers in the carribean waters.5. Concerning the air units Nato decides for the strategy to send a squadron US F-15 from Keflavik to North 7-8 and a squadron UK F4s to North 5-6 on patrol to detect and intercept Soviet reconnaissance aircraft and bombers early. Moreover, one german squadron of Atlantique MPs is sent to the Baltic sea to cover TF Viking against suspected soviet submarines in the area.6. As a final preparatory step, NATO is moving the US carrier Enterprise into TF Mustang and the carrier America into TF Aegis. Both should additionally secure their TF and especially the cnovoys against enemy bomber attacks.SOVIETS1. The soviets have decided to purchase the SAM and ECM technologies, which greatly enhances their survivability of their bombers (ECM tech) and surface units (SAM tech). This is a daring move as their spy marker has now been reduced by 4 to only 1 for the rest of the campaign.2. They use the option to move assets from the Far East over to Europe and take the Backfire regiment from the "Destroyed" box and swap it with two badger regiments from the baltic. The backfires are stationed on the Kola peninsula.3. No strike units are moved to another base.4. Only the older artillery cruiser "Sverdlov" is moved from the Baltic fleet to the North Fleet, in preparation of a soviet amphibious invasion of Norway.5. A Tango and a Yankee class submarine group are placed in East 6 with the intention of hunting the suspected Churchill submarines there. A Foxtrot (Mid 3), a Juliett (Mid 5) and another Juliett (W 7-8) group are stationed next to NATO TFs with the intention of attacking them as soon as possible and therefore hopefully catch them off guard. Furthermore, a Kilo and an Echo II group have been moved to North 5-6, to attempt the breakthrough into the atlantic.6. The soviets form TF Borodino with all available assets the Northern Fleet can offer and move them into the Barents sea, to attempt an amphibious invasion ASAP near Narvik/Bodo.7. Weather is very good at the beginning of the conflict, with only the Mediterranean in zone 3-4 experiencing a heavy storm.8. The tattletale rolls have following effects: TF Aegis (2D10): 5 and 10 = Good Detection; TF Hammer (1D10): 9 = Good Detection; TF Mustang (1D10): 2 = Undetected; TF Black (1D10): 2 = Undetected; TF Viking (1D10): 6 = Poor DetectionThat's it for now. Next time I'll upload the first moves from both sides.
